title: C# OOP Interview Answers
content:
C# OOP Interview Answers

Corrected, interview-ready reference for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: Start with a one-line definition, explain the key difference, and finish with a practical example from your experience.

# A1. What are the four principles of OOP?

Interview-ready answer

The four main principles of object-oriented programming are abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism.

• Abstraction: It hides unnecessary implementation details and exposes only the functionality required by the caller. In C#, abstraction can be achieved using interfaces and abstract classes.

• Encapsulation: It combines data and the methods that operate on that data within a single unit, such as a class. It also protects the data by using access modifiers and controlled access through properties or methods.

• Inheritance: It allows a child class to reuse and extend the members of a parent class, which promotes code reusability.

• Polymorphism: It allows the same method, interface, or operation to have different behaviour depending on the object. Method overloading is compile-time polymorphism, and method overriding is runtime polymorphism.

Short version to remember

Abstraction hides implementation, encapsulation protects data, inheritance promotes reusability, and polymorphism allows one contract or method name to have different behaviours.

# A2. What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class?

Interview-ready answer

An interface mainly defines a contract that implementing classes must follow. An abstract class can define a contract and also provide shared implementation and state for related classes.

• A class can implement multiple interfaces but can inherit from only one class.

• An abstract class can contain fields, properties, constructors, abstract methods, and implemented methods.

• An interface can contain methods, properties, events, and indexers. Modern C# also supports default interface method implementations, but an interface does not store normal instance state like a class.

• Interface members are public by default for the implementing contract. Modern C# allows additional access modifiers in some interface-member scenarios, so saying "interfaces can use only public" is not fully correct.

• Interfaces are commonly used with dependency injection to achieve loose coupling. Abstract classes are useful when related classes need both a common contract and shared behaviour.

Short version to remember

I use an interface when different classes need the same contract and loose coupling. I use an abstract class when closely related classes also need shared code or state.

# A3. Explain method overloading and method overriding.

Interview-ready answer

Method overloading means defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists, such as a different number, type, or order of parameters. It is resolved at compile time.

Method overriding means that a child class provides a new implementation of a virtual or abstract method declared in the base class. It uses the override keyword and is resolved at runtime.

Important clarification

Changing only the return type is not enough to overload a method; the parameter list must be different.

# A4. Why should we use throw; instead of throw ex;?

Interview-ready answer

Inside a catch block, throw; rethrows the current exception while preserving its original stack trace. This makes it easier to identify the actual method and line where the exception occurred. Using throw ex; resets the stack trace from the current location and can hide useful debugging information.

Code example

try
{
    ProcessRequest();
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    _logger.LogError(ex, "Request processing failed");
    throw; // Preserves the original stack trace
}

# A5. Where have you used OOP concepts in your projects?

Interview-ready answer based on your experience

In my .NET applications, I used OOP concepts to separate responsibilities across controllers, services, repositories, and models. For example, controllers handled HTTP requests, service classes contained business logic, and repository or data-access classes handled SQL Server operations.

We used interfaces for services and repositories so that implementations could be injected using dependency injection. This provided abstraction and loose coupling. Encapsulation was used by keeping validation and business rules inside the relevant classes instead of exposing data directly.

Inheritance and polymorphism were used where related components shared common behaviour or implemented the same interface differently. In my L3-support role, understanding these layers helped me trace production issues from the controller to the business and database layers, analyse logs, identify the root cause, and coordinate or implement fixes.

Safer short version

I have used OOP mainly to separate controller, business, and data-access responsibilities. I used interfaces and dependency injection for loose coupling, encapsulation for business rules, and polymorphism where multiple implementations followed the same contract. This structure also helped me troubleshoot production issues during L3 support.

Speaking practice: Read each short version aloud twice. Then explain it again without looking at the document. Aim for understanding rather than memorising every word.

title: C# Collections and Generics
content:
C# Collections and Generics

Corrected, interview-ready answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: Explain why you selected a collection, not only what the collection does. Mention ordering, uniqueness, lookup speed, and whether the size can change.

# A1. What are generics, and what are their benefits?

Interview-ready answer

Generics allow us to create reusable, type-safe classes, interfaces, methods, and collections that can work with different data types. The required type is supplied through a type parameter such as T.

• They provide compile-time type safety and help detect type errors early.

• They reduce explicit casting because the expected type is already known.

• They can improve performance for value types by avoiding unnecessary boxing and unboxing.

• They allow one reusable implementation to work with multiple data types.

List<int> employeeIds = new();
List<string> employeeNames = new();

Short version to remember

Generics provide reusable and type-safe code. They reduce casting, catch type errors at compile time, and can avoid boxing and unboxing.

# A2. Compare an array and List<T>.

Interview-ready answer

An array has a fixed length after it is created, whereas List<T> can grow or shrink dynamically. I use an array when the number of elements is fixed and known in advance. I use List<T> when I need to add or remove items.

• An array uses the Length property; List<T> uses the Count property.

• Both arrays and List<T> preserve the order of their elements.

• Arrays support multidimensional structures; List<T> is normally a dynamic one-dimensional collection.

Important correction

A typed array does not normally require casting. For example, an element from int[] is already an int. Casting is commonly required with non-generic collections such as ArrayList or Hashtable, because they store values as object.

int[] fixedNumbers = { 10, 20, 30 };
int number = fixedNumbers[0]; // No casting required
List<int> dynamicNumbers = new() { 10, 20, 30 };
dynamicNumbers.Add(40);

Short version to remember

An array has a fixed length, while List<T> can grow or shrink. Both are type-safe and ordered. I choose an array for fixed-size data and List<T> when the size can change.

# A3. When would you use a dictionary instead of a list?

Interview-ready answer

I use Dictionary<TKey, TValue> when data can be represented as unique key-value pairs and fast lookup by key is required. A dictionary provides average O(1) lookup by key, whereas searching an unsorted list is generally O(n).

For example, if I frequently need to find an employee by employee ID, I can use the employee ID as the dictionary key and the Employee object as the value.

Dictionary<int, Employee> employeesById = new();
employeesById[101] = employee;

if (employeesById.TryGetValue(101, out Employee result))
{
    Console.WriteLine(result.Name);
}

Important interview points

• Dictionary keys must be unique.

• Use TryGetValue when a key may not exist; it avoids a KeyNotFoundException.

• Use a list when ordering, sequential processing, or duplicate items are more important than key lookup.

Short version to remember

I use a dictionary for unique key-value data and fast lookup by key. I use a list for an ordered sequence of items or when duplicate values are allowed.

# A4. Compare Dictionary and Hashtable.

Interview-ready answer

Dictionary<TKey, TValue> is a generic and type-safe collection. Hashtable is a legacy, non-generic collection that stores keys and values as object.

• Dictionary validates key and value types at compile time.

• Hashtable usually requires casting when values are retrieved.

• Hashtable can cause boxing and unboxing when value types are stored or retrieved.

• Dictionary is normally preferred in modern C# applications.

• Neither collection allows duplicate keys.

Short version to remember

Dictionary is generic, type-safe, and preferred in modern C#. Hashtable stores data as object, often requires casting, and is mainly found in older applications.

# A5. Which collection would you use to remove duplicate values?

Interview-ready answer

I would use HashSet<T> when I need to store only unique values because it does not allow duplicate elements. It also provides fast membership checks in the average case.

List<int> numbers = new() { 10, 20, 10, 30, 20 };
HashSet<int> uniqueNumbers = new(numbers);

// Result: 10, 20, 30

Important interview points

• HashSet<T> guarantees uniqueness, but you should not depend on it for a particular item order.

• If I only need a distinct list as part of a LINQ query, I can use Distinct().ToList().

List<int> uniqueList = numbers.Distinct().ToList();

Short version to remember

I use HashSet<T> when uniqueness is the main requirement because it does not store duplicates. For a LINQ result, I can also use Distinct().

Speaking practice: Give the short answer first. If the interviewer asks further, explain the comparison and provide one practical example.

title: C# LINQ Interview Answers
content:
C# LINQ Interview Answers

Corrected, interview-ready answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: Explain what the operator does, when the query executes, and whether the work happens in memory or is translated by a provider such as Entity Framework.

# A1. What is LINQ, and what are its benefits?

Interview-ready answer

LINQ stands for Language Integrated Query. It is a C# feature used to query, filter, sort, group, and transform data from collections, databases, XML, and other supported data sources using a consistent syntax.

• It provides compile-time type checking and IntelliSense support.

• It makes query code shorter, readable, and strongly typed.

• The same LINQ style can be used with different data sources through different providers.

List<int> evenNumbers = numbers
    .Where(x => x % 2 == 0)
    .ToList();

Short version to remember

LINQ is a C# feature for querying and transforming data from collections, databases, XML, and other sources using readable, strongly typed syntax.

# A2. Explain Where and Select.

Interview-ready answer

Where filters records based on a condition and keeps the original type or shape. Select projects or transforms each record into the required result, such as selecting one field or creating a new object.

var activeEmployees = employees
    .Where(x => x.IsActive);

var employeeNames = employees
    .Select(x => x.Name);

Short version to remember

Where filters records; Select transforms records or chooses the required fields.

# A3. FirstOrDefault versus SingleOrDefault.

Interview-ready answer

FirstOrDefault returns the first matching record. If no record is found, it returns the default value. If multiple records match, it still returns the first one.

SingleOrDefault returns the only matching record or the default value when there is no match. It throws an InvalidOperationException when more than one record matches.

Use FirstOrDefault when the first match is acceptable. Use SingleOrDefault when the business rule requires the result to be unique.

Short version to remember

FirstOrDefault allows multiple matches and returns the first. SingleOrDefault requires zero or one match and throws an exception for multiple matches.

# A4. What is deferred execution?

Interview-ready answer

Deferred execution means that many LINQ queries are defined first but are not executed immediately. They execute when the result is enumerated, such as in a foreach loop, or when an immediate-execution operator is called.

var query = employees.Where(x => x.IsActive); // Not executed yet

List<Employee> result = query.ToList();       // Executes here

Important correction

Deferred execution does not apply to every LINQ operator. ToList, ToArray, Count, Any, First, and similar terminal operations execute the query immediately.

Short version to remember

Deferred execution means a query is executed when it is enumerated or materialised, not necessarily when it is declared.

# A5. IEnumerable versus IQueryable.

Interview-ready answer

IEnumerable<T> is commonly used for in-memory collections and uses LINQ to Objects. Once the data has been materialised, further filtering generally happens inside the application.

IQueryable<T> represents a query that a provider, such as Entity Framework, can translate into another query language such as SQL. Filters applied before materialisation can therefore run in the database, so only the required data is returned.

IQueryable<Employee> query = dbContext.Employees
    .Where(x => x.IsActive);

List<Employee> result = await query.ToListAsync();

Important interview point

Apply filters before ToList or ToArray when using Entity Framework. Calling ToList first loads the data and makes later filtering in-memory.

Short version to remember

IEnumerable is mainly for in-memory iteration. IQueryable builds an expression that a provider can translate, for example into SQL, before the data is loaded.

# A6. Any versus Count for existence checks.

Interview-ready answer

I use Any when I only need to know whether at least one matching record exists. It can stop after finding the first match. Count determines the total number of matching records, which performs unnecessary work for a simple existence check.

With Entity Framework, Any is generally translated into an efficient SQL existence check, whereas Count asks the database to calculate the number of matches.

bool exists = employees.Any(x => x.Id == 101);      // Preferred
bool exists2 = employees.Count(x => x.Id == 101) > 0;

Short version to remember

Use Any for existence checks because it can stop at the first match; Count calculates all matches.

# A7. Explain Select and SelectMany.

Interview-ready answer

Select performs a one-to-one projection: each source element produces one result. SelectMany performs a one-to-many projection and flattens nested collections into one sequence.

var employeeLists = departments
    .Select(x => x.Employees);      // IEnumerable<List<Employee>>

var allEmployees = departments
    .SelectMany(x => x.Employees);  // IEnumerable<Employee>

Simple example

If every department has its own employee list, Select returns a collection of employee lists. SelectMany combines the employees from all department lists into one flat employee sequence.

Short version to remember

Select transforms each item and keeps nested collections nested. SelectMany transforms and flattens nested collections into one sequence.

Speaking practice: Give the short answer first. Then add the example only if the interviewer asks for more detail.

ASP.NET Core MVC Interview Answers
content:
ASP.NET Core MVC Interview Answers

Corrected, interview-ready answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: Explain the responsibility of each component and add one practical request-flow example.

# A1. What is MVC, and what are the responsibilities of its components?

Interview-ready answer

MVC is an architectural design pattern that separates an application into Model, View, and Controller components. This separation of concerns improves maintainability, testability, and organisation.

• Model represents application data, validation rules, and domain-related behaviour. Business logic is commonly placed in domain or service classes rather than directly in a controller.

• View presents data to the user and handles the user-interface representation.

• Controller receives requests, validates or coordinates input, calls the required services, and selects the response or view.

Important correction: a controller should coordinate the request flow; it should not contain large amounts of business logic.

# A2. ASP.NET MVC versus ASP.NET Core MVC

Interview-ready answer

Classic ASP.NET MVC runs on the .NET Framework, depends on System.Web, and is primarily Windows-based. Dependency injection is not built into the framework in the same way and is commonly added through a separate container.

ASP.NET Core MVC runs on modern .NET, is cross-platform, has built-in dependency injection, uses middleware instead of HTTP modules and handlers, and commonly uses appsettings.json with multiple configuration providers.

Short version: ASP.NET Core MVC is cross-platform, modular, high-performance, and includes built-in dependency injection.

# A3. Conventional routing versus attribute routing

Interview-ready answer

Conventional routing defines a general URL pattern centrally, usually in Program.cs. The framework uses route segments to determine the controller, action, and optional parameters.

app.MapControllerRoute(
    name: "default",
    pattern: "{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}");

Attribute routing defines routes directly on controllers and action methods using attributes such as Route, HttpGet, and HttpPost. It provides precise control and is commonly used for Web APIs.

[Route("employees")]
public class EmployeeController : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("{id}")]
    public IActionResult Details(int id) => View();
}

# A4. What are model binding and model validation?

Interview-ready answer

Model binding automatically maps incoming request values to action parameters or model properties. Values can come from route data, query strings, form fields, headers, or the request body.

Model validation checks the bound model against declared validation rules, such as data-annotation attributes or custom validators. In MVC, ModelState.IsValid is commonly checked before processing the request.

public class EmployeeViewModel
{
    [Required]
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

if (!ModelState.IsValid)
    return View(model);

Important correction: property validation is not a replacement for all business rules. Complex business validation commonly belongs in the service or domain layer.

# A5. What is dependency injection, and what are its benefits?

Interview-ready answer

Dependency injection is a design pattern in which a class receives its dependencies from an external provider instead of creating them manually. ASP.NET Core includes a built-in dependency-injection container.

• It reduces coupling between classes.

• It improves maintainability and allows implementations to be replaced easily.

• It makes unit testing easier because dependencies can be mocked or substituted.

builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmployeeService, EmployeeService>();

public EmployeeController(IEmployeeService employeeService)
{
    _employeeService = employeeService;
}

# A6. Explain Transient, Scoped, and Singleton lifetimes

Interview-ready answer

• Transient: a new instance is created each time the service is requested. It is suitable for lightweight, stateless services.

• Scoped: one instance is created per HTTP request and reused within that request. It is commonly used for business services and Entity Framework DbContext.

• Singleton: one instance is created for the application service provider and reused across requests and users. It must be thread-safe.

Important correction: Singleton does not mean one instance per user. Also avoid directly injecting a scoped service into a singleton because their lifetimes are incompatible.

# A7. ViewBag versus ViewData versus TempData

Interview-ready answer

ViewData is a dictionary used to pass data from a controller to a view during the current request. Values normally require casting when retrieved as a specific type.

ViewBag is a dynamic wrapper around ViewData. It also works only for the current request, but it uses dynamic property syntax and does not provide compile-time type checking.

TempData stores data temporarily and can survive a redirect. It normally remains available until it is read, although Peek and Keep can extend its availability.

For main page data, prefer a strongly typed view model. Use TempData for short-lived messages such as 'Employee created successfully' after a redirect.

# A8. View() versus RedirectToAction()

Interview-ready answer

View() renders a view as part of the current request. It does not create another browser request, and the browser URL remains unchanged. It is commonly used to redisplay a form when validation fails.

RedirectToAction() returns a redirect response, commonly HTTP 302. The browser then sends a new GET request to the specified action, so the URL can change.

After a successful POST, RedirectToAction is commonly used as part of the Post/Redirect/Get pattern to reduce duplicate form submissions.

# Quick Revision. Important points to remember

• MVC separates Model, View, and Controller responsibilities.

• ASP.NET Core MVC is cross-platform and has built-in dependency injection.

• Conventional routes are central patterns; attribute routes are declared on controllers or actions.

• Model binding maps request values; model validation checks declared rules.

• Scoped means one instance per HTTP request; Singleton means one shared application instance.

title: Middleware, Filters & Exception Handling
content:
Middleware, Filters & Exception Handling

Corrected, interview-ready answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: Clearly separate the HTTP middleware pipeline from the MVC filter pipeline.

# A1. What is middleware, and how does it work?

Interview-ready answer

Middleware is a component in the ASP.NET Core HTTP request pipeline that can inspect or modify an incoming request and outgoing response. It can execute logic before and after the next component.

A middleware normally calls the next middleware through RequestDelegate. It can also short-circuit the pipeline by returning a response without calling the next component.

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    // Before the next middleware
    await next();
    // After the next middleware
});

# A2. Why is middleware order important?

Interview-ready answer

Middleware executes in the order in which it is registered for the request and generally in reverse order for the response. Each component can affect whether later components execute.

• Global exception handling should be registered early so it can catch downstream exceptions.

• Authentication must run before authorization so the user identity is available.

• Routing must identify the endpoint before authorization evaluates endpoint requirements.

Short answer: incorrect middleware order can cause authentication, authorization, routing, or exception handling to behave incorrectly.

# A3. Explain Use, Run, and Map

Interview-ready answer

• Use adds middleware that can call the next component and can run logic before and after it.

• Run adds terminal middleware. It handles the request and does not call another middleware.

• Map creates a separate pipeline branch when the request path matches a specified path.

Important correction: Map does not merely forward a request to the next middleware; it branches the pipeline by path.

app.Map("/admin", admin =>
{
    admin.Run(context =>
        context.Response.WriteAsync("Admin area"));
});

# A4. What are MVC filters? Name the main filter types

Interview-ready answer

MVC filters execute at specific stages of the MVC action pipeline and allow cross-cutting logic to run before or after controller actions and results.

• Authorization filter: performs MVC-specific authorization checks.

• Resource filter: runs around most of the MVC pipeline and can support caching or short-circuiting.

• Action filter: runs before and after an action method.

• Exception filter: handles certain unhandled exceptions from the MVC action pipeline.

• Result filter: runs before and after an action result executes.

Important correction: Authentication and Response are not MVC filter types. Authentication is normally middleware; the relevant MVC type is an authorization filter.

# A5. Middleware versus filters

Interview-ready answer

Middleware works in the general HTTP pipeline and can apply to all requests. It primarily works with HttpContext and is suitable for concerns such as exception handling, authentication, request logging, correlation IDs, and security headers.

Filters work inside the MVC pipeline and have MVC-specific context for controllers, actions, arguments, results, and model state. They are suitable for logic that specifically surrounds MVC action execution.

Short version: middleware is HTTP-pipeline-wide; filters are MVC-specific.

# A6. What happens when local and global exception handling both exist?

Interview-ready answer

A method-level catch block handles only exception types that match its catch clauses. If it handles an exception and returns normally without rethrowing it, the global exception handler does not receive that exception.

If the exception is not matched locally, or the local catch uses throw; to rethrow it, the exception continues up the call stack and can be handled by the global exception middleware.

Important correction: the local handler is not always called first for every exception. It runs only when a matching local catch block exists.

# A7. How do you implement global exception handling?

Interview-ready answer

ASP.NET Core can use the built-in exception-handler middleware, commonly with ProblemDetails for APIs. A custom middleware can also wrap await _next(context) in try-catch, log the exception, map known exceptions to suitable status codes, and return a safe standard response.

builder.Services.AddProblemDetails();

app.UseExceptionHandler();

The exception middleware should be registered early. Production responses must not expose stack traces, SQL statements, internal paths, or sensitive information.

# A8. Exception filter versus exception middleware

Interview-ready answer

An exception filter works inside MVC and handles supported exceptions arising from controller actions or MVC result processing. It does not cover the complete HTTP pipeline.

Exception middleware surrounds downstream HTTP processing and can catch exceptions from later middleware and endpoints, including MVC. Therefore, middleware is generally preferred for application-wide exception handling.

# A9. Should every method contain try-catch?

Interview-ready answer

No. Writing try-catch in every method creates duplicate code and can hide or incorrectly swallow failures. Unexpected exceptions can normally be logged and converted into a standard response by the global handler.

Use a local try-catch when the method can recover, return a meaningful result for a known exception, add useful context, translate the exception into a domain-specific exception, or perform required cleanup.

When rethrowing, use throw; to preserve the original stack trace. Do not use throw ex;.

# Quick Revision. Important points to remember

• Middleware handles the HTTP pipeline; filters handle MVC-specific stages.

• Middleware order affects request and response behaviour.

• Use calls the next component, Run terminates, and Map branches by path.

• The main filters are authorization, resource, action, exception, and result filters.

• Handled local exceptions do not reach the global handler; unhandled or rethrown exceptions can.

• Use global middleware for unexpected exceptions and local catch blocks only when meaningful handling is possible.

title: Web API and REST Interview Answers
content:
# Web API and REST Interview Answers

## What is ASP.NET Web API?

ASP.NET Core Web API is used to build HTTP services that expose application data and operations to web, mobile and other clients. A well-designed API keeps controllers thin, puts business rules in services, validates requests, returns consistent HTTP responses and remains observable in production.

## What does REST mean?

REST is an architectural style built around resources, standard HTTP methods, stateless requests and cacheable responses. A resource is normally identified by a URI such as /api/orders/42. The server does not keep conversational client state between requests; each request contains the information needed to process it.

## HTTP methods and idempotency

GET reads a resource and should not change server state. POST normally creates a new resource or starts an operation and is not inherently idempotent. PUT replaces a complete resource and should be idempotent. PATCH applies a partial update. DELETE removes a resource and should produce the same final state when repeated.

## ControllerBase versus Controller

ControllerBase provides API-focused features such as routing, model binding, validation helpers and HTTP result methods. Controller also supports MVC views. For a JSON API, ControllerBase with the ApiController attribute is normally the clearer choice.

## IActionResult versus ActionResult<T>

IActionResult is useful when an action can return several response shapes. ActionResult<T> documents the successful response type while still allowing results such as NotFound, BadRequest or Unauthorized. For typed APIs, ActionResult<T> usually gives better readability and OpenAPI metadata.

## Model binding and validation

Model binding reads route values, query strings, headers and request bodies into action parameters or DTOs. Validation checks whether the request satisfies required rules. With ApiController, invalid model state can automatically produce a 400 response. Business validation should still live in the service layer.

## Important status codes

Return 200 for a successful read or update with a body, 201 with a Location header for successful creation, 204 for success without a body, 400 for invalid input, 401 for missing or invalid authentication, 403 for insufficient permission, 404 when a resource is absent, 409 for a state conflict and 500 for an unexpected server failure.

## Production API practices

Use global exception handling and a consistent Problem Details response. Add structured logging and a correlation identifier. Secure endpoints with authentication and policy-based authorization. Use pagination for large collections, cancellation tokens for long-running work, rate limiting to protect capacity, caching where staleness is acceptable, and API versioning when contracts must evolve without breaking clients.

## Interview-ready answer

I design APIs with thin controllers, DTO-based contracts and service-layer business logic. I use dependency injection, validation, authentication and authorization, meaningful status codes, global exception handling and structured logging. For production endpoints, I also consider pagination, cancellation, idempotency, rate limiting, caching, versioning and resilience for outbound calls.

## Quick revision

• REST is stateless and resource-oriented.
• GET is safe; PUT and DELETE should be idempotent.
• Use ControllerBase for APIs and ActionResult<T> for typed responses.
• Keep controllers thin and return consistent status codes.
• Treat security, validation, error handling and observability as part of API design.

title: Entity Framework Core Interview Answers
content:
Entity Framework Core Interview Answers

Corrected, interview-ready answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: Explain the concept first, mention when it is used, and add a small practical example.

# A1. What is Entity Framework Core, and what are its advantages?

Interview-ready answer

Entity Framework Core is an Object-Relational Mapper (ORM) for .NET applications. It allows us to interact with relational databases using C# objects and LINQ instead of writing SQL for every operation. EF Core converts LINQ queries into SQL and maps the returned rows to C# objects.

• It reduces repetitive data-access code and supports CRUD operations.

• It provides LINQ querying, change tracking, migrations, relationships, and asynchronous database operations.

# A2. What are DbContext and DbSet<T>?

Interview-ready answer

DbContext represents a session between the application and the database. It manages database connections, executes queries, tracks entity changes, and saves those changes. DbSet<T> represents a collection of a particular entity type and generally corresponds to a database table.

public class AppDbContext : DbContext
{
    public DbSet<Employee> Employees { get; set; }
}

# A3. Code First versus Database First

Interview-ready answer

In Code First, we create C# entity classes and configuration first, and then create or update the database schema using migrations. It is generally used for new applications when the development team controls the database design.

In Database First, the database already exists and entity classes plus DbContext are generated from it using scaffolding. It is generally used for legacy systems or when a DBA team manages the database.

# A4. What are migrations, and which commands are commonly used?

Interview-ready answer

Migrations keep the database schema synchronized with changes made to entity classes in the Code First approach. They describe schema operations such as creating tables, adding columns, and defining keys or relationships.

• Add-Migration <Name>: creates a new migration.

• Update-Database: applies pending migrations to the database.

• Remove-Migration: removes the latest migration when it has not been applied.

• Script-Migration: generates a SQL migration script.

Important correction: the command is Update-Database, not Update-Migration.

# A5. What is change tracking?

Interview-ready answer

Change tracking is an EF Core feature that tracks the state and property changes of entities loaded through DbContext. When SaveChanges() or SaveChangesAsync() is called, EF Core detects those changes and generates the required INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE commands.

• Common states are Added, Modified, Deleted, Unchanged, and Detached.

var employee = await context.Employees.FindAsync(1);
employee.Name = "Ashutosh";
await context.SaveChangesAsync();

# A6. What is AsNoTracking(), and when should it be used?

Interview-ready answer

AsNoTracking() tells EF Core not to track the entities returned by a query. It should be used for read-only operations when the returned data will not be modified and saved through the same DbContext. It reduces change-tracking overhead and can improve memory usage and query performance.

var employees = await context.Employees
    .AsNoTracking()
    .ToListAsync();

Use AsNoTracking() for GET APIs and reports, but not when you plan to modify the loaded entity and rely on automatic change tracking.

# A7. Explain eager loading, explicit loading, and lazy loading

Interview-ready answer

• Eager loading loads the main entity and required related data as part of the query, commonly using Include().

• Explicit loading loads the main entity first and then loads related data manually when it is required.

• Lazy loading automatically loads related data when a navigation property is accessed. It requires configuration and should be used carefully because it can cause many unexpected database queries.

var employees = await context.Employees
    .Include(e => e.Department)
    .ToListAsync();

Lazy loading can cause the N+1 query problem when a separate query is executed for each record's related data.

# A8. What is the difference between Include() and ThenInclude()?

Interview-ready answer

Include() loads directly related data through a navigation property. ThenInclude() loads the next level of related data from an entity that was included previously.

var departments = await context.Departments
    .Include(d => d.Employees)
    .ThenInclude(e => e.Address)
    .ToListAsync();

In this example, Include() loads the employees of each department, and ThenInclude() loads the address of each employee.

Important correction: say ThenInclude(), not 'the include'.

# A9. What happens when SaveChangesAsync() is called?

Interview-ready answer

SaveChangesAsync() detects changes in tracked entities, determines their states, generates the required SQL commands, and executes them asynchronously against the database. For a relational database provider, multiple changes in one SaveChanges call are normally applied within a transaction. After a successful save, tracked entity states are generally changed to Unchanged and generated values such as identity keys may be populated.

SaveChangesAsync() does not make the complete HTTP request asynchronous; it asynchronously waits for the database operation.

# A10. How can EF Core query performance be improved?

Interview-ready answer

• Use AsNoTracking() for read-only queries.

• Use Select() to retrieve only the required columns.

• Apply Where() before materializing the query with ToListAsync().

• Use pagination with Skip() and Take() for large result sets.

• Avoid unnecessary Include() calls and prevent N+1 queries.

• Use suitable database indexes and inspect generated SQL for slow queries.

• Use async query methods for scalable I/O, while remembering that async does not make the SQL itself faster.

var employees = await context.Employees
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Where(e => e.IsActive)
    .Select(e => new { e.Id, e.Name })
    .Take(50)
    .ToListAsync();

# Quick Revision. Important points to remember

• DbContext manages a database session; DbSet<T> represents an entity collection.

• Code First uses entities and migrations; Database First scaffolds code from an existing database.

• Tracking supports updates; AsNoTracking() is intended for read-only queries.

• Include() loads direct relationships; ThenInclude() loads the next relationship level.

• SaveChangesAsync() detects tracked changes and sends the required SQL commands to the database.

• Good performance depends on projection, filtering, pagination, indexes, and controlled related-data loading.

title: Repository Pattern and Unit of Work
content:
Repository Pattern and Unit of Work

Corrected, interview-ready answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: Keep business rules in services and persistence queries in repositories; explain where one logical operation begins and ends.

# A1. What is the Repository Pattern, and why is it used?

Interview-ready answer

The Repository Pattern separates business logic from data-access logic. A service depends on a repository abstraction rather than directly depending on DbContext or database-specific code. It supports separation of concerns, loose coupling, reusable queries, Dependency Inversion, and easier unit testing.

public interface IEmployeeRepository
{
    Task<Employee?> GetByIdAsync(int id);
    Task AddAsync(Employee employee);
}

# A2. Responsibilities of controller, service, and repository

Interview-ready answer

• Controller: handles HTTP requests and responses, request-level validation, calls the service, and returns appropriate HTTP status codes.

• Service: applies or coordinates business rules, calls one or more repositories, and controls the business-operation flow.

• Repository: performs data-access operations, builds persistence queries, and adds, updates, or deletes entities.

A repository should not normally contain business rules such as promotion eligibility, pricing, or discount calculations.

# A3. Advantages and disadvantages of Repository Pattern

Interview-ready answer

• Advantages: separation of concerns, data-access abstraction, reduced coupling, reusable queries, and easier mocking of dependencies.

• Disadvantages: additional interfaces and classes, possible duplication of EF Core features, limited generic CRUD abstractions, and extra complexity when the repository adds no meaningful value.

Repository interfaces help unit testing, but mocked tests do not replace integration tests against the actual database provider.

# A4. What is a generic repository, and what are its limitations?

Interview-ready answer

A generic repository provides common operations such as GetById, GetAll, Add, Update, and Delete for multiple entity types. It reduces repeated CRUD code.

public interface IRepository<T> where T : class
{
    Task<T?> GetByIdAsync(int id);
    Task AddAsync(T entity);
    void Update(T entity);
}

Its limitation is that real applications need entity-specific queries and aggregate behaviour. A generic repository can become too weak, too broad, or merely duplicate DbSet<T>. A practical design may combine common CRUD with focused repositories such as IEmployeeRepository.

# A5. Should a repository return IQueryable<T>?

Interview-ready answer

Returning IQueryable<T> allows callers to compose filters, sorting, projections, and pagination that can be translated to SQL. This provides flexibility and avoids loading unnecessary data.

However, it leaks EF Core query behaviour outside the repository, reduces repository control, delays query execution, and allows other layers to create inefficient or provider-specific queries. Alternatives include focused repository methods, query objects, specifications, or returning projected results.

There is no universal rule. If IQueryable is exposed, define a clear architectural boundary and prevent controllers or unrelated layers from building uncontrolled persistence queries.

# A6. What is the Unit of Work Pattern?

Interview-ready answer

The Unit of Work Pattern coordinates changes made through multiple repositories and saves them as one logical operation. The repositories share the same DbContext, and SaveChangesAsync() is called once after all required changes are prepared.

await orderRepository.AddAsync(order);
product.ReduceStock(order.Quantity);
await paymentRepository.AddAsync(payment);

await unitOfWork.SaveChangesAsync();

If saving fails, the operation should not be left partially completed. For relational providers, EF Core normally uses a transaction for the changes in a single SaveChanges call when transactions are supported.

# A7. Repository versus Unit of Work

Interview-ready answer

A repository handles queries and data operations for an entity or aggregate. A Unit of Work coordinates changes across repositories, ensures they use the same persistence context, and controls when those changes are saved.

• Repository example: EmployeeRepository retrieves and modifies employee entities.

• Unit of Work example: employee, department, and audit changes are saved together through one DbContext.

DbSet<T> provides repository-like behaviour, while DbContext provides Unit-of-Work-like behaviour through change tracking and SaveChangesAsync().

# A8. Why create repositories when EF Core already provides DbContext and DbSet<T>?

Interview-ready answer

An additional repository may be useful when it provides application-specific queries, hides persistence details from the business layer, centralizes repeated data-access rules, or creates a clear architectural boundary. It can also make service dependencies easier to replace in focused unit tests.

A repository should not be created automatically for every entity. If it only wraps Add, Update, Delete, and Find without adding useful abstraction, it may duplicate EF Core and increase complexity.

Database-backed validation queries can be placed in focused repositories, but business validation decisions generally belong in the service or domain layer.

# A9. Where should SaveChangesAsync() be called?

Interview-ready answer

The location depends on the application architecture. Saving inside every repository method is simple for independent operations but makes it harder to coordinate multiple changes atomically.

For multi-step business operations, SaveChangesAsync() is commonly called at the service or Unit-of-Work boundary after all repositories have prepared their changes. This allows the related changes to be committed together.

Unit-of-Work boundary means the point where one complete business operation ends. For PlaceOrder, the boundary may include creating the order, reducing stock, recording payment, and then saving once.

# A10. Repository versus service layer

Interview-ready answer

A repository is responsible for data access: querying, adding, updating, and deleting entities. A service is responsible for business rules and workflow: validating business conditions, coordinating repositories, and deciding what should happen.

var employee = await repository.GetByIdAsync(id);

if (!employee.IsEligibleForPromotion)
    throw new BusinessException("Not eligible");

employee.Promote();

The repository retrieves the employee; the service decides whether promotion is allowed. The controller then converts the outcome into an HTTP response.

# Quick Revision. Important points to remember

• Repository handles persistence; service handles business rules.

• Generic repositories cover common CRUD but may need focused extensions.

• IQueryable is flexible but can leak query-building outside the repository.

• Unit of Work coordinates repositories that share one DbContext and save boundary.

• Use repositories when they add meaningful abstraction, not merely to wrap every DbSet method.

title: JWT Authentication and Authorization
content:
JWT Authentication and Authorization

Corrected, interview-ready answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: Authentication identifies the user; authorization determines what that authenticated user is permitted to do.

# A1. Authentication versus authorization

Interview-ready answer

Authentication verifies who the user is, usually by validating credentials or a token. Authorization determines what an authenticated user is allowed to access or perform, based on roles, claims, or policies.

Simple example: login is authentication; checking whether the user may delete an employee is authorization.

# A2. What is JWT, and why is it used?

Interview-ready answer

JWT stands for JSON Web Token. It is a compact token format commonly used to represent an authenticated user's identity and claims when securing APIs. After login, the client sends the token with later requests, and the API validates it before allowing access.

More precisely, JWT is a token format. ASP.NET Core's bearer authentication validates it; authorization then uses its claims to make access decisions.

# A3. What are the three parts of a JWT?

Interview-ready answer

• Header: contains metadata such as the token type and signing algorithm.

• Payload: contains claims such as user ID, username, role, issuer, audience, and expiration time.

• Signature: is calculated from the encoded header and payload using a signing key. It allows the API to detect modification and verify that a trusted issuer signed the token.

Base64Url(Header).Base64Url(Payload).Signature

# A4. What are claims?

Interview-ready answer

Claims are statements about a subject, usually the authenticated user. Examples include user ID, username, role, email, permissions, issuer, audience, and token expiration. ASP.NET Core can use role or permission claims during authorization.

new Claim(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier, user.Id.ToString());
new Claim(ClaimTypes.Role, "Admin");

# A5. JWT authentication flow

Interview-ready answer

• The user submits credentials to the login endpoint over HTTPS.

• The server validates the credentials and generates a short-lived access token; it may also issue a refresh token.

• The client stores the tokens using an appropriate secure strategy.

• The client sends the access token as Authorization: Bearer <token> with protected API requests.

• The authentication middleware validates the signature, issuer, audience, and expiration. Authorization then evaluates roles, claims, or policies.

# A6. [Authorize] versus [AllowAnonymous]

Interview-ready answer

[Authorize] requires the request to satisfy an authorization policy. Without additional parameters, it normally requires an authenticated user. It can also require a role or named policy. [AllowAnonymous] bypasses authorization for that endpoint, even when the controller has [Authorize], and is commonly used for login or public endpoints.

[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]
[HttpDelete("{id}")]
public IActionResult Delete(int id) { ... }

# A7. Access token versus refresh token

Interview-ready answer

An access token is short-lived and is sent to protected APIs. A refresh token is longer-lived and is sent only to a token-refresh endpoint to obtain a new access token. Refresh tokens should be stored securely, tracked server-side when revocation or rotation is required, assigned an expiration, and rotated after use.

A refresh token does not have to be stored specifically in SQL Server; it may be stored in any suitable secure server-side data store.

# A8. What happens when an access token expires?

Interview-ready answer

The API rejects the expired access token and normally returns 401 Unauthorized. The client can call the refresh endpoint with a valid refresh token to obtain a new access token. If the refresh token is missing, revoked, or expired, the user must log in again.

# A9. 401 Unauthorized versus 403 Forbidden

Interview-ready answer

• 401 Unauthorized: authentication is missing or has failed—for example, the access token is missing, invalid, or expired.

• 403 Forbidden: authentication succeeded, but the user does not have the required role, claim, policy, or permission.

Although the name '401 Unauthorized' can be confusing, it normally indicates an authentication problem.

# A10. Is JWT encrypted, and can it contain sensitive data?

Interview-ready answer

A standard signed JWT is not encrypted. Its header and payload are Base64Url-encoded and can be decoded by anyone who obtains the token. The signature protects integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality. Therefore, passwords, secrets, and sensitive personal information should not be placed in the payload.

# A11. Where should browser clients store tokens?

Interview-ready answer

There is no universally safe storage location; the choice depends on the application and threat model. localStorage is simple but JavaScript can read it, so an XSS vulnerability can expose the token. For many browser applications, a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookie is safer against token theft through JavaScript, although cookie-based authentication requires appropriate CSRF protection.

Interview answer: explain the trade-off. Do not claim that localStorage is always the recommended or completely secure option.

# A12. How is logout implemented with stateless JWT authentication?

Interview-ready answer

The client deletes its access token. The server also revokes or deletes the associated refresh token so it cannot be used to obtain another access token. A previously issued access token normally remains valid until its short expiration unless the system maintains a token denylist, validates a user security version, or uses another server-side revocation check.

Practical design: short-lived access tokens plus rotated, server-side revocable refresh tokens limit the logout and compromise window.

# Quick Revision. Important points to remember

• Authentication identifies the user; authorization controls access.

• A JWT signature provides integrity and issuer verification, not encryption.

• Validate signature, issuer, audience, and expiration.

• 401 means authentication failed; 403 means authenticated but insufficient permission.

• Access tokens should be short-lived; refresh tokens should support secure storage, rotation, expiration, and revocation.

• Browser token storage is a security trade-off: localStorage has XSS risk; cookies require CSRF controls.

title: Caching in ASP.NET Core
content:
Caching in ASP.NET Core

Corrected, interview-ready answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Language correction: use caching, cache, and cached—not catching, chache, or catched.

# A1. What is caching, and why is it used?

Interview-ready answer

Caching is a technique used to store frequently accessed data temporarily so it can be retrieved faster. It improves response time and scalability while reducing repeated database queries, external API calls, and expensive calculations.

# A2. In-memory versus distributed caching

Interview-ready answer

In-memory caching stores data in the memory of an application instance. It is very fast and simple, but each instance has a separate cache, and its data is lost when that instance restarts.

Distributed caching stores data in an external shared cache that multiple application instances can access. It is suitable for load-balanced applications, although it adds network communication, serialization, and operational complexity.

Distributed cache is normally shared among application instances or servers—not necessarily among unrelated applications.

# A3. When should Redis be used instead of IMemoryCache?

Interview-ready answer

Redis is appropriate when an application runs on multiple instances and they need a shared cache. It is also useful when cached data should not depend on the lifetime of one application instance, or when centralized expiration, atomic operations, distributed sessions, or distributed coordination are required.

// Single application instance
builder.Services.AddMemoryCache();

// Multiple instances using a shared Redis cache
builder.Services.AddStackExchangeRedisCache(options => { ... });

# A4. Explain the cache-aside pattern

Interview-ready answer

In the cache-aside pattern, the application first checks the cache. If the data is available, it returns the cached value. Otherwise, it retrieves the data from the database, stores it in the cache with an expiration, and returns it.

if (cache.TryGetValue(key, out Product product))
    return product;

product = await repository.GetByIdAsync(id);
cache.Set(key, product, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));
return product;

# A5. Cache hit versus cache miss

Interview-ready answer

• Cache hit: the requested data is available in the cache and can be returned immediately.

• Cache miss: the requested data is unavailable, so the application retrieves it from the original data source and may then cache it.

# A6. Absolute versus sliding expiration

Interview-ready answer

Absolute expiration removes an entry after a fixed period, regardless of how often it is accessed. Sliding expiration renews the expiration window whenever the entry is accessed.

They can be combined: sliding expiration removes inactive data, while absolute expiration prevents frequently accessed data from remaining cached forever.

new MemoryCacheEntryOptions
{
    SlidingExpiration = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2),
    AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)
};

# A7. What is cache invalidation?

Interview-ready answer

Cache invalidation means removing or updating cached data when the original data changes. It is important because an outdated cache entry can cause the application to return stale data.

A common approach is: update the database successfully, then remove the related cache key so the next read reloads fresh data.

# A8. What should and should not be cached?

Interview-ready answer

• Good candidates: frequently accessed and infrequently changing data, reference data, expensive query results, configuration data, and suitable external API responses.

• Poor or risky candidates: passwords or sensitive data, rapidly changing data, data that must always be current, rarely accessed data, and very large objects.

User-specific data requires correctly isolated cache keys so one user never receives another user's cached result.

# A9. Data caching versus response or output caching

Interview-ready answer

Data caching stores application data such as products, configuration, or query results. Response caching stores an entire HTTP response according to HTTP caching rules. Output caching is server-controlled endpoint-response caching and gives the application more direct control over caching policies.

Do not cache personalized responses unless the policy varies correctly by user or another relevant identifier.

# A10. What is stale data?

Interview-ready answer

Stale data is outdated cached data. It occurs when the original data has changed but the cache still contains and returns the older version.

# A11. What is a cache stampede?

Interview-ready answer

A cache stampede occurs when a popular cache entry expires and many concurrent requests simultaneously query the database to rebuild the same entry. This can cause a sudden increase in database load.

• Possible controls: per-key locking or single-flight execution.

• Refresh important entries before expiration.

• Add a small random variation to expiration times so many keys do not expire together.

# A12. How do you avoid returning an old product after an update?

Interview-ready answer

After successfully updating and committing the product in the database, remove the related cached entry. The next request will retrieve the latest product from the database and cache it again. Another option is to update the cache immediately after the database update, but invalidation is often simpler and safer.

await repository.UpdateAsync(product);
await unitOfWork.SaveChangesAsync();

cache.Remove($"product:{product.Id}");

Invalidate only after the database update succeeds. Removing the cache first can allow another request to reload the old database value before the transaction commits.

# Quick Revision. Important points to remember

• IMemoryCache belongs to one application instance; distributed cache is shared.

• Cache-aside means check cache, load on miss, store, and return.

• Absolute expiration is fixed; sliding expiration renews on access.

• Cache invalidation prevents stale data after writes.

• Protect against cache stampedes for popular or expensive entries.

• Cache only when the performance benefit is greater than the consistency and operational cost.

title: Logging and Observability in ASP.NET Core
content:
Logging and Observability in ASP.NET Core

Corrected, interview-ready answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: Explain how logs, metrics, and traces work together. For production incidents, describe a systematic investigation rather than saying only, 'I will check the logs.'

# A1. What is logging, and why is it important?

Interview-ready answer

Logging records information about application execution, important business or technical events, warnings, and errors. It helps developers monitor behaviour, troubleshoot production problems, audit important actions, and understand what happened before and during a failure.

# A2. What are the ASP.NET Core log levels?

Interview-ready answer

• Trace: extremely detailed diagnostic information; usually disabled in production.

• Debug: development and troubleshooting information.

• Information: normal application events, such as an operation completing.

• Warning: an unexpected condition that has not stopped the application.

• Error: a failure in the current operation.

• Critical: a severe failure that may affect the entire application or require immediate action.

• None: disables logging for a category.

Your original list was almost correct, but Critical and None were missing.

# A3. What is structured logging?

Interview-ready answer

Structured logging records important values as named, searchable properties rather than constructing only a plain-text message. This makes it easier to filter, group, and analyze logs by fields such as OrderId, UserId, or CorrelationId.

logger.LogInformation(
    "Order {OrderId} created for customer {CustomerId}",
    order.Id, customer.Id);

Prefer message templates. Avoid string interpolation because it turns useful properties into plain text and may perform unnecessary formatting.

# A4. What is ILogger<T>?

Interview-ready answer

ILogger<T> is the built-in logging abstraction injected through dependency injection. The generic type creates a logging category, normally the class name. Application code logs through this abstraction, while configured providers send the records to destinations such as Console, Debug, EventLog, Application Insights, or another logging platform.

# A5. What is a correlation ID?

Interview-ready answer

A correlation ID is an identifier attached to all logs related to one request or logical business operation. It allows engineers to search for the identifier and reconstruct the flow across middleware, services, repositories, and—when propagated—multiple services.

In distributed tracing, TraceId and SpanId provide a standard way to correlate work across services. Do not create a separate custom ID when the existing trace context meets the requirement.

# A6. How should exceptions be logged and rethrown?

Interview-ready answer

Pass the exception object to the logging method so the log provider captures its type, message, inner exception, and stack trace. Use throw; when rethrowing inside a catch block because it preserves the original stack trace. Avoid throw ex;, which resets the visible throw location.

catch (Exception ex)
{
    logger.LogError(ex, "Failed to process order {OrderId}", orderId);
    throw;
}

Avoid logging the same exception at every layer. Usually log it once where it is handled or at the centralized boundary.

# A7. What information should not be logged?

Interview-ready answer

• Passwords, PINs, secret keys, and connection-string secrets.

• Access tokens, refresh tokens, session identifiers, and authentication cookies.

• Full credit-card or bank-account details.

• Sensitive personal, medical, or regulated information unless explicitly protected and required.

• Complete request or response bodies without reviewing, filtering, masking, and size limits.

Use redaction or masking where a partial value is genuinely needed, and restrict access and retention for production logs.

# A8. How should unhandled exceptions be handled?

Interview-ready answer

Unhandled exceptions should normally be processed by centralized exception-handling middleware. It can log the exception once, attach request or trace context, return a consistent ProblemDetails response, and avoid exposing internal exception details to the client. Method-level try-catch should be used when the method can recover, translate, retry, or add meaningful context.

# A9. How can a correlation ID be implemented?

Interview-ready answer

A custom middleware can read a trusted correlation header or create an identifier, add it to the response, place it in a logging scope, and call the next middleware. It must be registered in Program.cs early enough for later logs to contain the value. In distributed applications, the trace context should also be propagated to outgoing HTTP calls.

using (logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object>
{
    ["CorrelationId"] = correlationId
}))
{
    await next(context);
}

# A10. Logs versus metrics versus traces

Interview-ready answer

• Logs: detailed event records, such as a validation failure or exception with context.

• Metrics: numerical measurements aggregated over time, such as request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, CPU, and memory usage.

• Traces: show the end-to-end path and timing of a request across services and operations. Each operation is represented by a span.

Metrics show that a problem exists; traces show where time or failure occurred; logs explain detailed context around it.

# A11. How would you investigate a slow API?

Interview-ready answer

I would first confirm the endpoint, time window, frequency, affected users, and latency percentile. I would use metrics or APM data to verify the slowdown, then use a trace or correlation ID to break the request into controller, service, database, and external-call timings. I would check SQL execution plans and wait times, outbound HTTP duration, thread-pool or connection-pool pressure, CPU, memory, and recent deployments. After identifying the bottleneck, I would reproduce it, implement the fix, and compare the same measurements afterward.

A timestamp tells when something happened; it does not by itself show which operation consumed the time. Record durations or use tracing spans.

# A12. How would you troubleshoot a production error?

Interview-ready answer

I would begin with the alert or user report and determine the impact, affected endpoint, time window, environment, status code, and correlation or trace ID. I would check dashboards and logs for exceptions and patterns, follow the trace to the failing component, review dependency health and recent deployments or configuration changes, and verify database or infrastructure symptoms. If impact is high, I would mitigate first through rollback, feature disablement, failover, or another approved recovery action. I would then reproduce the issue safely, fix and test it, monitor recovery, document the root cause, and add preventive monitoring or tests.

This answer uses your L3 support experience positively while still demonstrating developer-level diagnosis and ownership.

# Quick Revision. Important points to remember

• Use the correct log level and structured message templates.

• Never log secrets, tokens, passwords, or unchecked request bodies.

• Correlate logs with request trace context and avoid duplicate exception logging.

• Centralized exception middleware handles unexpected failures consistently.

• Use metrics to detect, traces to locate, and logs to explain.

title: Unit Testing with xUnit and Moq
content:
Unit Testing with xUnit and Moq

Study-ready interview answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: Unit tests verify business behaviour in isolation. Integration tests verify that components—including EF Core, routing, middleware, serialization, and databases—work together.

# A1. What is unit testing, and why is it used?

Interview-ready answer

Unit testing verifies a small unit of code, normally a method or class, in isolation from external systems. It helps detect regressions, documents expected behaviour, supports safe refactoring, and improves confidence when business logic changes. Good unit tests are fast, independent, repeatable, and focused on one behaviour.

# A2. Explain the Arrange–Act–Assert pattern

Interview-ready answer

• Arrange: create the system under test, configure dependencies, and prepare inputs.

• Act: execute the method or behaviour being tested.

• Assert: verify the returned value, state change, exception, or meaningful dependency interaction.

// Arrange
var calculator = new Calculator();

// Act
var result = calculator.Add(10, 20);

// Assert
Assert.Equal(30, result);

# A3. [Fact] versus [Theory] in xUnit

Interview-ready answer

[Fact] represents one test scenario without input parameters. [Theory] represents a parameterized test that runs the same behaviour with multiple data sets supplied through sources such as [InlineData], [MemberData], or [ClassData].

[Theory]
[InlineData(18, true)]
[InlineData(17, false)]
public void IsAdult_ReturnsExpected(int age, bool expected)
{
    Assert.Equal(expected, service.IsAdult(age));
}

# A4. What is mocking, and why is it used?

Interview-ready answer

Mocking creates a controlled test replacement for a dependency such as a repository, HTTP client abstraction, clock, or message publisher. It allows the test to control dependency results, simulate failures, and verify important interactions without using a real database, network, or external service.

Mock interfaces or replaceable boundaries—not simple value objects or every internal method. Excessive mocking makes tests coupled to implementation details.

# A5. Setup() versus Verify() in Moq

Interview-ready answer

Setup() configures how a mock behaves when a member is called—for example, which employee a repository returns. Verify() confirms that a meaningful interaction occurred with the expected arguments and frequency.

repositoryMock
    .Setup(x => x.GetByIdAsync(1))
    .ReturnsAsync(employee);

repositoryMock.Verify(
    x => x.GetByIdAsync(1),
    Times.Once);

Prefer asserting observable outcomes. Use Verify when the interaction itself is important, such as publishing an event or sending a notification.

# A6. Unit test versus integration test

Interview-ready answer

• Unit test: checks one unit in isolation, replaces external dependencies, runs quickly, and identifies business-logic failures precisely.

• Integration test: checks multiple real components together and may verify the HTTP pipeline, model binding, authentication, EF Core mappings and queries, or a test database.

Both are required. Mocked tests cannot prove that a LINQ expression translates correctly to SQL or that middleware and routing are configured correctly.

# A7. Why should a unit test not normally use a real database?

Interview-ready answer

A real database makes a test slower and dependent on infrastructure, schema, network, existing data, and cleanup. That changes it from a unit test into an integration test. For unit tests, inject a repository or data-access abstraction and provide a controlled replacement. Use separate integration tests to validate real EF Core and database behaviour.

# A8. How do you test an asynchronous method?

Interview-ready answer

Make the test method return Task and await the operation. Configure asynchronous dependencies with ReturnsAsync or ThrowsAsync. Avoid async void because the test framework cannot reliably await it or capture its failures.

[Fact]
public async Task GetAsync_EmployeeExists_ReturnsEmployee()
{
    repositoryMock.Setup(x => x.GetByIdAsync(1))
                  .ReturnsAsync(employee);

    var result = await service.GetAsync(1);

    Assert.Equal(employee.Id, result!.Id);
}

# A9. How do you test exceptions?

Interview-ready answer

Use Assert.Throws<TException> for synchronous code and Assert.ThrowsAsync<TException> for asynchronous code. Verify the exception type and, when part of the contract, important properties or message content.

var exception = await Assert.ThrowsAsync<BusinessException>(
    () => service.PlaceOrderAsync(request));

Assert.Equal("INSUFFICIENT_STOCK", exception.Code);

# A10. What should and should not be unit tested?

Interview-ready answer

• Test business rules, calculations, branching behaviour, validation decisions, error paths, boundary values, and important state changes.

• Test meaningful interactions when the interaction is part of the behaviour, such as saving once or publishing an event.

• Do not usually test automatic properties, framework internals, trivial pass-through code, private implementation details, or third-party library behaviour.

Test through the public behaviour. If private logic is complex, consider whether it represents a separate responsibility that should be extracted into a testable class.

# A11. What is code coverage? Does 100% guarantee quality?

Interview-ready answer

Code coverage measures which statements or branches were executed while tests ran. It helps identify untested areas, but 100% coverage does not guarantee correct assertions, meaningful scenarios, good design, or protection against defects. Coverage is a diagnostic metric, not the final quality goal.

Prioritize business-critical paths, boundary conditions, failures, and regression risks over chasing a percentage.

# A12. How does dependency injection improve testability?

Interview-ready answer

Dependency injection provides a class's dependencies from outside instead of allowing the class to construct concrete implementations. A unit test can therefore supply mocks, stubs, or fakes for repositories and external services, control their behaviour, and test the class in isolation.

var repositoryMock = new Mock<IEmployeeRepository>();
var service = new EmployeeService(repositoryMock.Object);

# Quick Revision. Important points to remember

• Use Arrange–Act–Assert and descriptive test names such as Method_Scenario_ExpectedResult.

• [Fact] is one scenario; [Theory] runs one behaviour with multiple data sets.

• Mock external boundaries, but avoid coupling every test to internal implementation details.

• Await asynchronous operations and use ThrowsAsync for asynchronous exceptions.

• Unit and integration tests solve different problems; one does not replace the other.

• Meaningful scenarios and assertions matter more than a coverage percentage.

title: SQL Server Fundamentals Interview Answers
content:
SQL Server Fundamentals Interview Answers

Corrected, interview-ready answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: Define the concept, explain the difference, and add one practical SQL example when possible.

# A1. Primary key versus foreign key

Interview-ready answer

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. Its values must be unique and cannot be NULL. A table can have only one primary-key constraint, although the key can contain multiple columns. A foreign key creates a relationship with a primary or unique key and maintains referential integrity. A table can contain multiple foreign keys, and foreign-key values can repeat and may allow NULL.

Important correction: a primary key creates a unique index. It is clustered by default only when no clustered index already exists and NONCLUSTERED is not specified.

# A2. Explain INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and FULL OUTER JOIN

Interview-ready answer

• INNER JOIN returns only matching records from both tables.

• LEFT JOIN returns every record from the left table and matching records from the right table. Missing right-side values are returned as NULL.

• FULL OUTER JOIN returns matching records plus unmatched records from both tables. Columns from the missing side contain NULL.

SELECT e.EmployeeName, d.DepartmentName
FROM Employees e
LEFT JOIN Departments d
    ON e.DepartmentId = d.DepartmentId;

# A3. WHERE versus HAVING

Interview-ready answer

WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and aggregation. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has been applied. WHERE should normally be used for non-aggregate row conditions, while HAVING is used for aggregate conditions such as COUNT(*) > 5.

SELECT DepartmentId, COUNT(*) AS EmployeeCount
FROM Employees
WHERE IsActive = 1
GROUP BY DepartmentId
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

# A4. DELETE versus TRUNCATE versus DROP

Interview-ready answer

• DELETE removes selected or all rows and supports a WHERE clause. It normally does not reset the identity value and can activate DELETE triggers.

• TRUNCATE removes all rows, does not support WHERE, normally resets the identity value, and does not activate row-level DELETE triggers. It cannot normally truncate a table referenced by an active foreign key.

• DROP removes the complete table, including its rows, definition, indexes, constraints, and object permissions.

In SQL Server, DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP can be rolled back when they are executed inside an explicit transaction.

# A5. What is a stored procedure, and what are its advantages?

Interview-ready answer

A stored procedure is a named collection of SQL statements stored in the database. It can accept parameters, return result sets, use output parameters, control transactions, handle errors, and perform SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations. It is executed using EXEC or EXECUTE.

• It supports reusable and centralized database logic.

• It provides parameterization and permission control.

• It can reduce network round trips for multi-statement operations and may reuse a cached execution plan.

Avoid saying that a stored procedure is always precompiled or always faster. SQL Server can compile, cache, reuse, or recompile its execution plan.

# A6. What is a view, and does it physically store data?

Interview-ready answer

A view is a named SQL query that behaves like a virtual table. A regular view stores the query definition rather than a separate physical copy of its result. The underlying tables are accessed when the view is queried. Views can hide query complexity, expose selected columns, and provide controlled access to data.

Exception: an indexed view physically stores indexed result data and must satisfy additional SQL Server requirements.

# A7. Stored procedure versus function

Interview-ready answer

• A stored procedure can return multiple result sets, output parameters, and a return-status code. A function returns one defined result, but that result can be a scalar value or a table with multiple rows and columns.

• Stored procedures can modify permanent data using INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. User-defined functions have stricter restrictions and cannot normally modify permanent database data.

• Stored procedures support TRY...CATCH. User-defined functions do not.

• A function can be used inside an appropriate SELECT statement or expression; a stored procedure is executed separately using EXEC.

# A8. What is a CTE, and when is it used?

Interview-ready answer

A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a temporary named result set defined using WITH. Its scope is limited to the single statement immediately following it. It improves the readability of complex queries and can be recursive, which makes it useful for hierarchical data such as employee-manager relationships.

WITH HighSalaryEmployees AS
(
    SELECT EmployeeId, EmployeeName, Salary
    FROM Employees
    WHERE Salary > 50000
)
SELECT * FROM HighSalaryEmployees;

A CTE is not limited to small datasets and does not automatically store results or improve performance. Performance depends on the execution plan.

# A9. Temporary table versus table variable

Interview-ready answer

A local temporary table is created with #TableName and stored in tempdb. It is visible within the current session, supports indexes and statistics, and is commonly more suitable for larger or complex intermediate results.

A table variable is declared with DECLARE @TableName TABLE. It also uses tempdb, but its scope is limited to the current batch, stored procedure, or function. It is commonly suitable for smaller and simpler intermediate results.

A temporary table is not always faster. Choose by testing the row count, query complexity, indexing needs, statistics, and execution plan.

# A10. What is normalization? Explain 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF

Interview-ready answer

Normalization is the process of organizing data into related tables to reduce duplication, improve consistency, and prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies.

• First Normal Form (1NF): each column contains an atomic value, and repeating groups are removed.

• Second Normal Form (2NF): the table is in 1NF, and every non-key column depends on the complete composite key, not only part of that key.

• Third Normal Form (3NF): the table is in 2NF, and non-key columns do not depend on other non-key columns; they depend only on the key.

Easy memory rule: 1NF - one value in one cell; 2NF - depend on the whole key; 3NF - depend on nothing except the key.

# Quick Revision. Important points to remember
