• Primary keys uniquely identify rows; foreign keys maintain relationships and referential integrity.

• WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters grouped results.

• DELETE removes rows, TRUNCATE clears a table, and DROP removes the table object.

• A regular view stores a query definition; a CTE exists for only the immediately following statement.

• Functions return a defined scalar or table result; stored procedures support broader operations.

• Normalization reduces duplication: atomic values, full-key dependency, and no non-key dependency.

title: SQL Server Indexing, Transactions and Performance
content:
SQL Server Indexing, Transactions and Performance

Corrected, interview-ready answers for Ashutosh Parmar

Interview tip: For performance questions, explain what you would measure before adding or changing an index.

# A1. What is an index, and what are its advantages and disadvantages?

Interview-ready answer

An index is a database structure that helps SQL Server locate data efficiently without scanning the entire table. It can improve SELECT, filtering, sorting, grouping, and join performance.

• Advantages: faster reads, more efficient filtering and joins, and optional uniqueness enforcement.

• Disadvantages: additional storage and maintenance overhead during INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations.

An index does not always make a query faster. Its value depends on selectivity, query patterns, table size, and the number of returned rows.

# A2. Clustered index versus nonclustered index

Interview-ready answer

A clustered index determines the logical order of rows, and its leaf level contains the table's data pages. A table can have only one clustered index. A primary key creates one by default only when no clustered index exists and NONCLUSTERED is not specified.

A nonclustered index is a separate structure containing index-key values and row locators. A table can have multiple nonclustered indexes. The locator is generally the clustered key for a clustered table or a Row Identifier (RID) for a heap.

Important correction: a clustered index still consumes storage for its root and intermediate index pages. The limit of 999 nonclustered indexes is a system maximum, not a recommendation.

# A3. Index seek versus index scan

Interview-ready answer

An index seek navigates through an index to a specific key or key range. It is generally efficient for selective queries. An index scan reads a large portion or all of an index. A scan may be appropriate when the table is small or the query needs a large percentage of its rows.

A seek is not automatically good and a scan is not automatically bad. Compare returned rows, logical reads, elapsed time, and the complete execution plan.

# A4. What is a composite index, and why is column order important?

Interview-ready answer

A composite index contains multiple key columns. Column order matters because queries generally benefit most when they filter or join using the leading columns of the index. This is commonly called the leftmost-prefix principle.

CREATE INDEX IX_Employees_Department_Status
ON Employees(DepartmentId, IsActive);

This index can efficiently support DepartmentId alone or DepartmentId together with IsActive. It may not efficiently seek when a query filters only by IsActive. Choose the order from real predicates, joins, sorting, and selectivity.

# A5. Included columns and covering indexes

Interview-ready answer

Included columns are non-key columns stored at the leaf level of a nonclustered index. They are not part of its searchable or sortable key. A covering index contains every column required by a query as either a key or included column, allowing SQL Server to return the result without accessing the base table or clustered index.

CREATE INDEX IX_Employees_Email
ON Employees(Email)
INCLUDE (EmployeeName, DepartmentId);

Included columns can reduce key lookups and I/O, but wide covering indexes consume storage and increase write overhead.

# A6. What is an execution plan, and what should be checked?

Interview-ready answer

An execution plan shows the operators and access methods SQL Server uses or expects to use for a query. An estimated plan is produced without executing the query; an actual plan includes runtime information after execution.

• Check table scans and index scans on large tables, but do not assume every scan is a problem.

• Review index seeks, key lookups, join operators, sorts, filters, warnings, spills, and implicit conversions.

• Compare estimated rows with actual rows because large differences can indicate inaccurate statistics or estimation problems.

• Consider missing-index suggestions, but validate them against existing indexes and write overhead before creating anything.

# A7. What is a transaction? Explain ACID

Interview-ready answer

A transaction is a logical unit of work in which either all required operations succeed and are committed or a failure causes them to be rolled back.

• Atomicity: all operations succeed or all are rolled back - all or nothing.

• Consistency: the transaction moves the database from one valid state to another while respecting rules and constraints.

• Isolation: concurrent transactions are controlled so they do not incorrectly interfere with each other.

• Durability: after a transaction is committed, its changes remain saved even after a crash or restart, subject to durability configuration.

English correction: the property is Atomicity, not Automacity.

# A8. Explain transaction-isolation levels

Interview-ready answer

• Read Uncommitted: permits dirty reads and provides the least isolation.

• Read Committed: prevents dirty reads, but non-repeatable reads and phantom reads may still occur. It is the traditional SQL Server default when snapshot options have not changed the behavior.

• Repeatable Read: prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads, but phantom rows may still occur.

• Serializable: prevents dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads but can increase blocking.

• Snapshot: reads row versions rather than ordinary locked data, reducing reader-writer blocking; it requires row-version storage and update conflicts can occur.

# A9. Blocking versus deadlock, and how to reduce deadlocks

Interview-ready answer

Blocking occurs when one transaction holds a lock and another transaction waits for it. Blocking can be normal, although long blocking may indicate long transactions, poor queries, or missing indexes.

A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions form a circular wait: each holds a resource required by another. SQL Server detects the cycle and terminates one transaction as the deadlock victim.

• Access tables and resources in a consistent order.

• Keep transactions short and update only required rows.

• Create appropriate indexes and avoid user interaction inside transactions.

• Add safe retry handling for deadlock-victim errors where appropriate.

Important correction: multiple transactions accessing the same resource can cause blocking; it becomes a deadlock only when there is a circular wait.

# A10. What happens to an identity value after rollback?

Interview-ready answer

If an INSERT generates an identity value and the transaction is later rolled back, the row is removed but the consumed identity value is normally not restored or reused. The next successful INSERT may therefore produce a higher value and leave a gap.

BEGIN TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO Employees(EmployeeName) VALUES ('Amit');
ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;

Identity columns generate values; they do not guarantee gap-free numbering.

# Quick Revision. Slow-query optimization checklist

• Identify and reproduce the slow query; collect a baseline.

• Review the actual execution plan, logical reads, duration, and row estimates.

• Check indexes, SARGable filters, joins, lookups, sorts, and unnecessary SELECT * or DISTINCT.

• Use appropriate filtering and pagination, and investigate blocking or waits.

• Measure again after each change instead of assuming that an added index fixed the problem.

title: Advanced C# Concepts
content:
GUIDE 01

Advanced C# Concepts

Language behaviour, memory, delegates, records, iterators and resource management

LEVEL Senior .NET — FOCUS Interview-ready — USE Study + revision

This guide targets the C# questions that distinguish a senior developer from someone who only remembers syntax. Focus on explaining behaviour, trade-offs and practical use cases rather than memorizing definitions.

# What you should be able to explain

• Explain value and reference semantics without repeating the inaccurate “stack versus heap” shortcut.

• Choose correctly among ref, out and in, and recognize boxing allocations.

• Use delegates, events, records, nullable reference types and iterators appropriately.

• Separate garbage collection from deterministic resource cleanup.

• Diagnose managed memory retention and copy-related bugs.

# Value and reference semantics

A value-type variable contains its value. Assigning it normally copies that value. A reference-type variable contains a reference; assigning it copies the reference, so both variables can point to the same object. Storage location depends on context, so “value types are always on the stack” is not a reliable rule.

int a = 10;
int b = a;
b = 20;             // a is still 10

var e1 = new Employee { Name = "Ashutosh" };
var e2 = e1;
e2.Name = "Rahul"; // e1.Name is also Rahul

## Passing parameters

• ref: The caller initializes the variable; the method can read and replace the original variable.

• out: The caller need not initialize it; the method must assign it before returning. Common in TryParse-style APIs.

• in: Passes by readonly reference. It can reduce copying for large structs but should be used only after measuring or when intent is clear.

• default: C# passes arguments by value. For a reference type, the copied value is the reference, not the entire object.

static bool TryFind(int id, out Employee? employee)
{
    employee = repository.Find(id);
    return employee is not null;
}

# Boxing, generics and allocations

Boxing copies a value type into an object or interface representation. Unboxing extracts the exact boxed value type. Repeated boxing creates allocations and additional garbage-collection work.

int number = 10;
object boxed = number;    // boxing
int result = (int)boxed; // unboxing

// (long)boxed throws InvalidCastException because the boxed type is int.

Generic collections such as List<int> retain the type and avoid the boxing that older non-generic collections such as ArrayList require.

# Delegates, Func, Action and events

A delegate is a type-safe reference to a compatible method. It enables callbacks and passing behaviour as data. Func returns a value, Action returns void, and Predicate<T> accepts T and returns bool.

Func<int, int, int> add = (x, y) => x + y;
Action<string> log = message => Console.WriteLine(message);
Predicate<int> isAdult = age => age >= 18;

An event wraps a delegate with controlled publication. External code can subscribe or unsubscribe, but normally only the declaring class can raise the event. Long-lived publishers can keep subscribers alive, so unsubscribe or use an appropriate weak/lifecycle pattern.

public event EventHandler<OrderCreatedEventArgs>? OrderCreated;

private void OnCreated(int id) =>
    OrderCreated?.Invoke(this, new OrderCreatedEventArgs(id));

# Extension methods, records and nullability

An extension method is a static method in a static class whose first parameter uses this. It adds call-site convenience but does not modify the original type. A matching instance method has priority.

public static class StringExtensions
{
    public static bool HasValue(this string? value) =>
        !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value);
}

A class normally uses reference equality unless equality is overridden. A record class is a reference type designed for data-centric models and provides value-based equality. Records support with-expressions but are not automatically deeply immutable when they contain mutable members.

public record EmployeeDto(int Id, string Name);
var updated = original with { Name = "Rahul" };

Nullable reference types are compile-time analysis. string means “expected non-null”; string? permits null. The null-forgiving operator (!) only suppresses a warning and performs no runtime validation.

# Iterators, disposal and garbage collection

yield return creates an iterator. Execution is normally deferred until enumeration, so database access or exceptions can occur later than the method call. Multiple enumeration can repeat the work.

static IEnumerable<int> Even(IEnumerable<int> values)
{
    foreach (var value in values)
        if (value % 2 == 0)
            yield return value;
}

IDisposable provides deterministic cleanup for resources such as streams, connections and handles. using compiles to cleanup logic that runs even when an exception occurs. IAsyncDisposable and await using support asynchronous cleanup.

await using var connection = new SqlConnection(connectionString);
await connection.OpenAsync(cancellationToken);

The garbage collector reclaims unreachable managed objects. New objects usually begin in Generation 0; survivors may move to Generations 1 and 2. Large objects use the large object heap. Do not normally call GC.Collect(); it can increase pauses and disrupt GC heuristics.

• GC manages managed memory; Dispose releases resources deterministically.

• Static collections, event subscriptions, timers and unbounded caches can retain reachable objects indefinitely.

• A shallow copy duplicates only the top-level object; nested references remain shared. A deep copy duplicates the required mutable object graph.

# Additional senior-level language points

• IEnumerable<T>: Pull-based synchronous enumeration; LINQ-to-Objects or deferred pipelines.

• IAsyncEnumerable<T>: Asynchronous streaming with await foreach; useful when items arrive over time.

• Span<T>: A stack-only view over contiguous memory that can reduce allocations in hot paths; it cannot be stored in ordinary heap objects.

• readonly struct: Prevents mutation of instance fields and can clarify value-object intent.

• Pattern matching: Use type, property, relational and switch patterns to express branching safely and readably.

# Interview-ready questions and answers

Q1. What is the difference between value and reference types?

Value-type variables contain values and assignments normally copy those values. Reference-type variables contain references and assignments copy the reference, so variables can point to the same object. The difference is semantic; their physical storage depends on context.

Q2. How do ref, out and in differ?

ref requires initialization and permits reading and writing the original variable. out does not require caller initialization but the method must assign it. in passes by readonly reference, mainly useful for large structs or expressing non-mutation.

Q3. Why can boxing hurt performance?

Boxing creates an object allocation and copies the value. Frequent boxing increases allocation rate and GC pressure; unboxing also requires the exact compatible value type.

Q4. What is a delegate?

A delegate is a type-safe method reference. I use it for callbacks, event handlers, LINQ predicates and strategies where behaviour must be supplied to another component.

Q5. Delegate versus event?

A delegate can be invoked by code that can access it. An event exposes controlled subscription while invocation normally remains inside the publisher.

Q6. Class versus record?

A class is a general reference type with reference equality by default. A record is optimized for data models with generated value-based equality and with-expressions, but nested mutable members can still change.

Q7. What does the null-forgiving operator do?

It suppresses nullable-analysis warnings. It does not check or change the runtime value, so misuse can still produce NullReferenceException.

Q8. When does a yield iterator execute?

When it is enumerated, not usually when the iterator method is called. Each enumeration can repeat its work.

Q9. Why use using when .NET has GC?

GC eventually recovers managed memory, but using calls Dispose deterministically so scarce resources such as connections and handles are released promptly.

Q10. Should GC.Collect be called manually?

Normally no. The GC chooses collection timing using runtime heuristics. Manual collection can cause expensive pauses and is reserved for rare, measured scenarios.

Q11. Can managed code leak memory?

It can retain memory unnecessarily when objects remain reachable through static collections, event handlers, timers, tasks or unbounded caches. GC cannot collect reachable objects.

Q12. Shallow versus deep copy?

A shallow copy creates a new top-level object but shares nested references. A deep copy duplicates the necessary nested mutable objects so changes do not cross between copies.

# Common interview traps

• Saying every value type is on the stack and every reference type is on the heap.

• Using ref or in without a demonstrated need.

• Assuming records are deeply immutable.

• Using ! as if it performs a null check.

• Expecting Dispose to destroy an object or expecting GC to close a resource immediately.

# 60-second revision checklist

• Value vs reference semantics

• ref / out / in

• boxing and generics

• delegates / events / Func / Action

• records and nullable references

• yield and deferred execution

• IDisposable vs GC

• managed retention and copy depth

title: Common Design Patterns
content:
GUIDE 02

Common Design Patterns

Practical patterns, trade-offs and .NET examples without pattern overengineering

LEVEL Senior .NET — FOCUS Interview-ready — USE Study + revision

Patterns are reusable design vocabulary, not rules to force into every system. In interviews, explain the problem, the pattern, its trade-off and a real project use case.

# What you should be able to explain

• Recognize when a pattern solves a real coupling or variation problem.

• Explain common creational, structural and behavioural patterns.

• Connect dependency injection and ASP.NET Core features to patterns.

• Avoid replacing simple code with unnecessary abstraction.

# How to discuss a pattern

State the design problem or source of change.

Describe the participating objects and responsibility split.

Give one small implementation example.

Explain the cost: extra types, indirection, state or operational complexity.

Say when a simpler approach would be better.

# Creational patterns

## Factory Method

A factory centralizes object creation and hides concrete selection from callers. Use it when creation depends on runtime data or requires setup.

public interface INotifier { Task SendAsync(string text); }

public sealed class NotifierFactory
{
    public INotifier Create(Channel channel) => channel switch
    {
        Channel.Email => new EmailNotifier(),
        Channel.Sms => new SmsNotifier(),
        _ => throw new NotSupportedException()
    };
}

## Builder

A builder constructs a complex object step by step and can make optional configuration readable. It is useful when constructors become ambiguous or object creation must enforce stages.

## Singleton

A singleton provides one instance for an application boundary. ASP.NET Core DI can register singleton lifetime, but the service must be thread-safe and must not capture scoped dependencies. Global mutable state makes testing and concurrency harder.

# Structural patterns

## Adapter

An adapter translates one interface into the interface expected by the application. Use it to isolate a third-party payment, storage or legacy API.

public sealed class LegacyPaymentAdapter : IPaymentGateway
{
    private readonly LegacyClient _client;
    public Task<PaymentResult> ChargeAsync(Money amount) =>
        MapAsync(_client.MakePayment(amount.Value));
}

## Decorator

A decorator wraps the same abstraction to add behaviour without changing the core implementation. Logging, caching, validation and retry are common examples.

public sealed class CachedProductService : IProductService
{
    private readonly IProductService _inner;
    private readonly IMemoryCache _cache;
    public Task<Product?> GetAsync(int id) =>
        _cache.GetOrCreateAsync($"product:{id}", _ => _inner.GetAsync(id));
}

## Facade

A facade provides one simplified interface over several subsystems. An OrderFacade might coordinate inventory, payment and notification, while keeping the controller thin.

# Behavioural patterns

## Strategy

Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind one interface. DI can select a pricing, tax, export or notification strategy.

public interface IDiscountStrategy
{
    decimal Calculate(Order order);
}

public sealed class PremiumDiscount : IDiscountStrategy
{
    public decimal Calculate(Order order) => order.Total * 0.10m;
}

## Observer

Observer notifies subscribers when state changes. .NET events implement an in-process form; message brokers provide cross-process asynchronous notification with different reliability concerns.

## Template Method

A base class defines an algorithm skeleton and derived classes override selected steps. Prefer composition/strategy when inheritance would tightly couple behaviour.

## Chain of Responsibility

A request passes through ordered handlers. ASP.NET Core middleware and MediatR pipeline behaviours are familiar examples.

# Patterns already present in ASP.NET Core

• Dependency Injection: Inversion of Control plus configured lifetimes.

• Middleware pipeline: Chain of Responsibility.

• Options pattern: Typed configuration separated from consumers.

• ILogger providers: Abstraction with provider/adaptor implementations.

• IHostedService: Hosted lifecycle abstraction for background work.

• MVC filters: Cross-cutting pipeline/decorator-like behaviour around actions.

Repository and Unit of Work can be useful at domain boundaries, but EF Core DbContext already provides repository-like sets and a unit-of-work transaction boundary. Add custom abstractions only when they express meaningful domain operations or improve testability without hiding useful query capabilities.

# Interview-ready questions and answers

Q1. What is a design pattern?

A design pattern is a named, reusable approach to a recurring design problem. It provides vocabulary and trade-offs, not copy-paste code.

Q2. Factory versus dependency injection?

A DI container creates and supplies registered dependencies. A factory makes a runtime creation decision or performs specialized construction. A factory can itself receive dependencies through DI.

Q3. When would you use Strategy?

When one business operation has multiple interchangeable algorithms, such as discounts, payment routing or export formats, and I want to add or select behaviour without expanding conditionals.

Q4. Decorator versus inheritance?

A decorator adds behaviour by composition around the same abstraction and can be combined dynamically. Inheritance fixes behaviour in a type hierarchy and creates stronger coupling.

Q5. Adapter versus Facade?

An adapter changes an interface so incompatible code can work together. A facade simplifies access to a complex subsystem without necessarily changing semantic compatibility.

Q6. What is Observer?

A publisher maintains or exposes subscriptions and notifies observers about an event. .NET events are in-process; brokers extend the concept across services with delivery and consistency concerns.

Q7. Why can Singleton be dangerous?

It is shared across requests, so mutable state needs synchronization. It can create hidden global coupling and cannot depend directly on scoped services.

Q8. What pattern is ASP.NET Core middleware?

It is primarily Chain of Responsibility: ordered components can act before and after the next component or terminate the pipeline.

Q9. Is Repository always required with EF Core?

No. DbContext and DbSet already provide relevant behaviours. I add repositories for meaningful aggregate operations or to protect domain boundaries, not as a mechanical wrapper around every EF method.

Q10. When is Template Method appropriate?

When several algorithms share a stable sequence and subclasses need controlled variation. If variation must be combined freely, Strategy is usually more flexible.

Q11. How do you avoid overengineering with patterns?

Start with the concrete source of change, apply the smallest abstraction that removes harmful coupling, and evaluate whether the added indirection pays for itself.

Q12. Give a production example of Decorator.

Wrap an IProductService with caching or metrics while leaving the core service unchanged. The decorator implements the same interface and delegates to the inner service.

# Common interview traps

• Listing pattern definitions without a problem or use case.

• Calling every service a singleton.

• Creating factories that only call new for one fixed type.

• Adding repository layers that merely duplicate EF Core.

• Confusing an in-memory event with a durable message broker.

# 60-second revision checklist

• Factory / Builder / Singleton

• Adapter / Decorator / Facade

• Strategy / Observer / Template Method

• Chain of Responsibility and middleware

• DI lifetimes and singleton safety

• Pattern trade-offs and overengineering

title: Clean Architecture and CQRS
content:
GUIDE 03

Clean Architecture and CQRS

Boundaries, dependency direction, use cases, commands, queries and reliable side effects

LEVEL Senior .NET — FOCUS Interview-ready — USE Study + revision

Clean Architecture protects business rules from infrastructure concerns. CQRS separates read intent from write intent. They can be used independently and should be adopted in proportion to system complexity.

# What you should be able to explain

• Explain the dependency rule and common layer responsibilities.

• Design use cases that do not depend on controllers or databases.

• Separate commands from queries without claiming that separate databases are mandatory.

• Handle validation, transactions and integration events reliably.

# The dependency rule

Source-code dependencies point inward toward business policy. The domain must not depend on EF Core, ASP.NET Core, messaging or a particular database. Infrastructure implements interfaces defined at an inner boundary.

• Domain: Entities, value objects, aggregates, domain rules and domain events.

• Application: Use cases, commands, queries, DTOs, validation and ports/interfaces.

• Infrastructure: EF Core, repositories, message broker, file storage and external API adapters.

• Presentation/API: HTTP endpoints, authentication, request mapping and response formatting.

The exact project names are less important than dependency direction and responsibility. Avoid moving ordinary CRUD code through many layers only to imitate a diagram.

# A use-case flow

POST /orders
  -> API maps request to CreateOrderCommand
  -> validator checks input
  -> handler loads domain data
  -> aggregate enforces business rules
  -> unit of work commits
  -> outbox records integration event
  -> API returns 201 Created

Controllers should translate transport concerns. Application handlers coordinate a use case. Domain objects protect invariants. Infrastructure performs technical I/O.

# CQRS fundamentals

CQRS means Command Query Responsibility Segregation. A command requests a state change and normally returns an identifier or result, not a rich read model. A query returns data and must not change business state.

public record CreateOrderCommand(int CustomerId,
    IReadOnlyList<OrderItemDto> Items) : IRequest<int>;

public record GetOrderQuery(int Id) : IRequest<OrderDto?>;

CQRS does not require MediatR, microservices, event sourcing or two databases. It can begin as separate handler classes over the same database. Separate read stores are an advanced scaling choice with eventual-consistency cost.

# Validation, behaviours and transactions

• Input validation: Check shape, required values and ranges near the application boundary.

• Business invariants: Keep rules such as “cannot ship an unpaid order” inside the domain model.

• Pipeline behaviours: Apply validation, logging, authorization or timing consistently around handlers.

• Transaction boundary: Usually one command/use case commits atomically. Avoid a database transaction around remote network calls.

• Cancellation: Pass CancellationToken through handlers and I/O calls.

public async Task<int> Handle(CreateOrderCommand command,
    CancellationToken ct)
{
    var order = Order.Create(command.CustomerId, command.Items);
    _db.Orders.Add(order);
    await _db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
    return order.Id;
}

# Domain events, integration events and outbox

A domain event represents something meaningful inside one domain model and can coordinate in-process reactions. An integration event is a stable contract published to other services.

Publishing to a broker after a database commit can fail, leaving data saved but no event sent. The transactional outbox stores the event in the same database transaction as the business change. A background publisher later sends it and marks it processed. Consumers must remain idempotent because delivery can repeat.

# When to use and when to simplify

• Good fit: Complex business rules, multiple adapters, long-lived systems, independent testability or very different read/write models.

• Simpler fit: Small CRUD service with few rules may use a clear layered structure without full CQRS or domain modelling.

• Warning sign: Hundreds of empty handlers, interfaces with one trivial implementation, and mapping the same DTO through many identical models.

# Interview-ready questions and answers

Q1. What is the main rule of Clean Architecture?

Dependencies point inward. Business policy does not depend on frameworks or infrastructure; outer layers implement interfaces required by inner use cases.

Q2. What belongs in the domain layer?

Entities, value objects, aggregate invariants, domain services and domain events that express business behaviour without technical I/O.

Q3. What belongs in the application layer?

Use-case orchestration: commands, queries, handlers, DTOs, validation, authorization decisions and abstractions for required I/O.

Q4. What is CQRS?

It separates operations that change state from operations that read state, allowing different models, validation and optimization for each responsibility.

Q5. Does CQRS require separate databases?

No. It can use separate handlers and models over one database. Separate read and write stores are optional and introduce synchronization and eventual consistency.

Q6. Command versus query?

A command expresses intent to change state and may fail due to business rules. A query returns data and should not modify business state.

Q7. Where should validation happen?

Request-shape validation belongs near the application boundary; business invariants belong in the domain. Database constraints provide a final integrity layer.

Q8. What is a MediatR pipeline behaviour?

A wrapper around request handling for cross-cutting concerns such as validation, logging, timing or transactions, similar to a decorator pipeline.

Q9. Domain event versus integration event?

A domain event coordinates behaviour inside a boundary. An integration event is a versioned external contract intended for other services.

Q10. Why use the outbox pattern?

It atomically records the business change and event-to-publish in one database transaction, preventing the gap between committing data and publishing a message.

Q11. How do you test Clean Architecture code?

Unit-test domain rules and handlers with controlled dependencies, then use integration tests for infrastructure adapters, EF queries, transactions and API composition.

Q12. When would you avoid full Clean Architecture?

For a small, short-lived CRUD service with little business complexity, the abstraction and mapping overhead may exceed its benefit. I keep boundaries clear but choose proportional structure.

# Common interview traps

• Saying Clean Architecture means a fixed number of projects.

• Putting EF attributes or HTTP models throughout the domain without considering coupling.

• Claiming CQRS always needs two databases or event sourcing.

• Opening distributed transactions around remote services.

• Publishing events after commit without handling the failure gap.

# 60-second revision checklist

• Dependency rule

• Domain / Application / Infrastructure / API responsibilities

• Command vs query

• Validation and transaction boundaries

• Domain vs integration events

• Transactional outbox and idempotency

• When simplicity is better

title: Advanced Web API: Pagination, Versioning and Rate Limiting
content:
GUIDE 04

Advanced Web API

Pagination, API versioning, rate limiting and production-ready HTTP contracts

LEVEL Senior .NET — FOCUS Interview-ready — USE Study + revision

A senior API answer should cover correctness, client experience, performance and operations. Pagination protects the service, versioning protects clients, and rate limiting protects capacity.

# What you should be able to explain

• Design stable paginated responses and compare offset with cursor pagination.

• Evolve APIs without silently breaking clients.

• Apply server-side rate-limiting policies and return useful HTTP responses.

• Connect validation, idempotency, caching and observability to API design.

# Pagination

Never return an unbounded large collection. Define a default page size, enforce a maximum, use a deterministic sort, and return navigation metadata appropriate for the client.

public sealed record PagedResult<T>(
    IReadOnlyList<T> Items,
    int Page, int PageSize, long TotalCount);

[HttpGet]
public async Task<ActionResult<PagedResult<ProductDto>>> Get(
    int page = 1, int pageSize = 25, CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    pageSize = Math.Clamp(pageSize, 1, 100);
    return Ok(await service.GetPageAsync(page, pageSize, ct));
}

## Offset pagination

Uses Skip/Take or OFFSET/FETCH. It is easy to jump to a page and can return a total count, but large offsets become expensive and concurrent inserts/deletes can cause duplicates or missed rows.

## Cursor/keyset pagination

Uses the last seen stable sort key, such as (CreatedAt, Id), to request the next set. It performs well for deep scrolling and behaves better with changing data, but arbitrary page jumps and exact total counts are harder.

WHERE (CreatedAt < @createdAt)
   OR (CreatedAt = @createdAt AND Id < @id)
ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC
FETCH NEXT @pageSize ROWS ONLY

# API versioning

Version when a change is contract-breaking: removing or renaming a field, changing meaning/type, tightening previously accepted input, or changing status/error behaviour clients rely on. Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes when possible.

• URL segment: /api/v1/orders. Visible and simple, but versions become part of resource URLs.

• Query string: /api/orders?api-version=1.0. Easy to test, less explicit in routing.

• Header: api-version: 1.0. Keeps URLs stable but is less visible.

• Media type: Accept: application/vnd.company.order-v2+json. Precise content negotiation but more complex.

Publish a deprecation policy, document supported versions, monitor usage, provide a migration guide and sunset only after clients have reasonable time to move. Internal APIs also have consumers and need governance.

# Rate limiting

Rate limiting restricts requests over time or concurrent work. Partition policies by client identity, API key, user, tenant or IP depending on the threat model. IP-only limits can punish users behind shared networks and are easy to evade.

• Fixed window: Simple count per time window; bursts can occur at boundaries.

• Sliding window: Smoother approximation using segments from the recent window.

• Token bucket: Tokens refill over time; controlled bursts are allowed.

• Concurrency limiter: Limits simultaneous work rather than requests per clock period.

builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(options =>
{
    options.RejectionStatusCode = StatusCodes.Status429TooManyRequests;
    options.AddFixedWindowLimiter("public-api", o =>
    {
        o.PermitLimit = 100;
        o.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1);
        o.QueueLimit = 0;
    });
});

app.UseRateLimiter();

[EnableRateLimiting("public-api")]
[HttpGet]
public IActionResult GetProducts() => Ok();

Return 429 Too Many Requests and, when possible, Retry-After or equivalent rate-limit metadata. Rate limiting is not a substitute for authentication, authorization, query optimization or autoscaling.

# Contract and reliability details

• Validation: Return consistent ProblemDetails with field errors; do not expose internal stack traces.

• Idempotency: GET, PUT and DELETE should follow HTTP semantics. For retryable POST operations, consider an idempotency key and stored result.

• Cancellation: Accept and propagate CancellationToken so abandoned requests stop unnecessary I/O.

• Caching: Use ETag/If-None-Match or output caching only when authorization and vary-by rules are correct.

• Observability: Record latency, status, route template, trace ID and dependency timings without logging secrets.

• OpenAPI: Keep request/response schemas, error cases, versions and authentication requirements discoverable.

# Interview-ready questions and answers

Q1. Why paginate an API?

To bound response size, query cost, memory use and network time. I set defaults and a maximum, use deterministic ordering and return navigation information.

Q2. Offset versus cursor pagination?

Offset is simple and supports page jumps but becomes slow at deep offsets and unstable under changes. Cursor pagination uses a stable last-seen key, scales better for sequential navigation and reduces duplicate/missing rows.

Q3. Why is deterministic sorting required?

Without a unique tie-breaker, rows with the same sort value can move between pages. I sort by a business field plus a unique key such as Id.

Q4. When should an API version change?

When a change breaks an existing client contract. Additive optional fields usually do not require a new major version, but removals, semantic changes and incompatible validation often do.

Q5. Which versioning approach is best?

There is no universal best choice. URL versions are easiest to see; headers or media types keep resource URLs stable. Consistency, tooling and client needs matter more than the mechanism.

Q6. How do you retire an API version?

Announce deprecation, publish dates and migration guidance, monitor client usage, communicate with owners, and remove only after the agreed sunset policy.

Q7. What status is returned when rate limited?

429 Too Many Requests, ideally with guidance such as Retry-After so a well-behaved client knows when to retry.

Q8. Fixed window versus token bucket?

Fixed window counts requests in discrete periods and can allow boundary bursts. Token bucket refills capacity continuously and permits a configured burst while controlling the long-term rate.

Q9. How should limits be partitioned?

By the identity that represents fair usage: user, tenant, subscription or API key. IP can be a fallback but is imperfect for shared networks and proxies.

Q10. How do you make POST retry-safe?

Use a client-supplied idempotency key, store the operation/result atomically, and return the original outcome for duplicate keys.

Q11. What should a production API error contain?

A stable ProblemDetails-style response with status, title, useful validation detail and trace ID. It should not expose stack traces, SQL or secrets.

Q12. Where should rate limiting be applied?

Often at an edge gateway for broad protection and in the service for business-aware policies. The layers should be coordinated so clients receive predictable behaviour.

# Common interview traps

• Using Skip/Take without an OrderBy.

• Allowing arbitrary page sizes.

• Versioning every additive change.

• Using only IP-based limits for authenticated multi-tenant APIs.

• Retrying a non-idempotent request without an idempotency design.

# 60-second revision checklist

• Bounded page size and deterministic order

• Offset vs cursor trade-offs

• Breaking vs additive changes

• Deprecation and sunset policy

• Fixed/sliding/token/concurrency limits

• 429 and Retry-After

• ProblemDetails, cancellation and idempotency

title: HttpClient Resilience, Retry and Circuit Breaker
content:
GUIDE 05

HttpClient and Resilience

IHttpClientFactory, timeouts, retry, circuit breaker and safe dependency calls

LEVEL Senior .NET — FOCUS Interview-ready — USE Study + revision

Remote calls fail differently from local method calls: they time out, return transient errors, partially succeed or complete after the caller gives up. Resilience must improve recovery without multiplying load or duplicate side effects.

# What you should be able to explain

• Use IHttpClientFactory and typed clients correctly.

• Classify transient versus permanent failures.

• Configure timeout, retry, circuit breaker and concurrency controls in a safe order.

• Preserve cancellation, idempotency and observability.

# Why IHttpClientFactory

Creating and disposing HttpClient for every request can churn connections and exhaust sockets. Keeping one client forever without handler rotation can retain stale DNS behaviour. IHttpClientFactory manages handler lifetimes, centralizes configuration and supports named or typed clients.

builder.Services.AddHttpClient<InventoryClient>(client =>
{
    client.BaseAddress = new Uri(configuration["Inventory:BaseUrl"]!);
    client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Accept.ParseAdd("application/json");
});

public sealed class InventoryClient(HttpClient http)
{
    public async Task<StockDto?> GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        using var response = await http.GetAsync($"stock/{id}", ct);
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        return await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<StockDto>(ct);
    }
}

# Failure classification and timeout

• Transient: Timeout, temporary network failure, 408, 429, and many 5xx responses may succeed later.

• Permanent/client error: Most 4xx responses represent invalid input or authorization and should not be blindly retried.

• Ambiguous: A timeout after sending a request does not prove the server failed; the operation may have completed.

Use an overall timeout budget and propagate CancellationToken. Avoid stacking unrelated timeouts that make diagnosis unclear. A client cancellation is not a dependency failure and should not be logged as an error by default.

# Retry with backoff and jitter

Retry only transient failures, use a small attempt limit, exponential backoff and jitter, and respect Retry-After. Immediate synchronized retries can amplify an outage into a retry storm.

• GET and other idempotent operations are generally safer to retry.

• POST payment/order creation requires an idempotency key or another deduplication mechanism.

• Do not retry validation failures, authentication failures or a known business rejection.

• Each attempt must fit within the total latency budget.

# Circuit breaker and isolation

A circuit breaker stops sending calls when failures cross a threshold. Closed allows calls, Open fails fast, and Half-open permits limited trial calls. It protects the dependency and caller from wasting resources; it does not repair the downstream service.

• Timeout: Bounds how long one attempt or the total operation can consume resources.

• Retry: Handles brief transient faults.

• Circuit breaker: Fails fast during a sustained fault.

• Concurrency/rate limiter: Prevents the caller from overwhelming a dependency.

• Fallback: Returns a degraded response only when stale/default data is semantically acceptable.

# .NET resilience pipeline

Modern .NET applications can use Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience to attach standard resilience handlers. Defaults must still be reviewed for the endpoint’s idempotency and latency requirements.

builder.Services
    .AddHttpClient<InventoryClient>()
    .AddStandardResilienceHandler(options =>
    {
        options.TotalRequestTimeout.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10);
        options.Retry.MaxRetryAttempts = 3;
        options.CircuitBreaker.SamplingDuration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
    });

Do not add multiple resilience handlers that accidentally retry each other. Log attempt number, final outcome, dependency name and duration; use tracing so all attempts belong to the same operation.

# Production checklist

• Validate BaseAddress, TLS and credentials through typed options at startup.

• Reuse clients from the factory; do not mutate shared default headers per request.

• Use HttpRequestMessage for request-specific headers and correlation context.

• Limit response body sizes and stream large responses when appropriate.

• Dispose HttpResponseMessage/streams and avoid logging secrets or complete sensitive bodies.

• Track dependency latency, failure rate, retry count, breaker state and saturation.

# Interview-ready questions and answers

Q1. Why not create HttpClient for every call?

Per-call creation can churn connections and lead to socket exhaustion. IHttpClientFactory reuses handlers safely and centralizes client configuration.

Q2. Named versus typed client?

A named client is retrieved by a string configuration name. A typed client wraps HttpClient in a domain-specific class, giving compile-time dependencies and a focused API.

Q3. What should be retried?

Only failures likely to be transient, such as selected network errors, timeouts, 408, 429 or 5xx responses, and only when the operation is idempotent or deduplicated.

Q4. Why exponential backoff with jitter?

Backoff reduces pressure while a dependency recovers; jitter prevents many callers from retrying at the same synchronized moments.

Q5. What is a circuit breaker?

It tracks recent failures and opens after a threshold, temporarily failing fast. After a break period it allows trial calls in half-open state and closes when recovery is confirmed.

Q6. Retry versus circuit breaker?

Retry handles a small transient fault for one operation. A circuit breaker responds to a broader sustained failure by stopping calls for a period.

Q7. Why can retrying POST be dangerous?

The first request may have succeeded even though the response was lost. Retrying can create duplicate orders or charges unless the operation uses an idempotency key or deduplication.

Q8. How do timeout and cancellation differ?

A timeout is a resilience policy budget. Cancellation can originate from the caller or request abort. Both should flow through I/O, but caller cancellation should not be treated as a downstream outage.

Q9. What is fallback?

A deliberate degraded result such as cached reference data. It is safe only when returning stale/default data preserves business meaning and is visible to operations.

Q10. How do you prevent retry storms?

Limit attempts, use exponential backoff with jitter, respect Retry-After, use circuit breaking and concurrency limits, and avoid nested retries across layers.

Q11. What do you monitor?

Dependency latency, status/failure type, timeouts, retries, breaker state, concurrent calls and trace correlation.

Q12. What is an ambiguous timeout?

The caller timed out but cannot know whether the server completed the operation. The design must reconcile or deduplicate rather than assuming failure.

# Common interview traps

• Retrying every exception and every 4xx.

• Retrying POST without idempotency.

• Setting an infinite or extremely long timeout.

• Adding retry at gateway, service and SDK without a total attempt budget.

• Treating a circuit breaker as a mechanism that fixes the dependency.

# 60-second revision checklist

• IHttpClientFactory and typed clients

• Transient vs permanent errors

• Timeout and CancellationToken

• Backoff, jitter and Retry-After

• Circuit states

• Idempotency and ambiguous results

• Metrics and trace context

title: Microservices Fundamentals
content:
GUIDE 06

Microservices Fundamentals

Service boundaries, data ownership, communication, consistency and operations

LEVEL Senior .NET — FOCUS Interview-ready — USE Study + revision

Microservices trade local simplicity for organizational and operational independence. A strong answer explains both benefits and distributed-system costs, and does not assume that every application should be split.

# What you should be able to explain

• Define a service boundary around business capability and ownership.

• Compare synchronous and asynchronous communication.

• Explain database-per-service, eventual consistency, Saga and outbox.

• Describe gateways, observability, deployment and failure isolation.

# What makes a microservice

• Owns a cohesive business capability and its data.

• Can be built, deployed and scaled independently within agreed contracts.

• Has a clear owner and operational responsibility.

• Communicates across a network and therefore assumes latency and partial failure.

• Avoids a shared database schema that lets other services bypass its rules.

Size is not measured by line count. A useful boundary often follows domain concepts and team ownership. Splitting too early creates a distributed monolith: many deployments but tightly coupled releases and shared data.

# Communication choices

## Synchronous

HTTP/gRPC provides an immediate response and is simple for request/response flows. The caller is coupled to downstream availability and latency, so use timeouts, cancellation, circuit breaking and limited call depth.

## Asynchronous

A broker decouples timing and absorbs bursts. It introduces eventual consistency, duplicate delivery, ordering constraints and more difficult tracing.

Use synchronous calls when the caller truly needs an immediate answer. Use messages for notifications, long-running workflows and decoupled state propagation. Avoid turning every method call into a network call.

# Data ownership and consistency

Each service owns its persistence and exposes contracts rather than database tables. Cross-service joins move to API composition, replicated read models or analytics pipelines.

• Saga: A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions. Choreography reacts to events; orchestration uses a coordinator.

• Outbox: Atomically stores business data and messages to publish.

• Inbox/idempotency: Records processed message IDs or uses unique business keys to tolerate duplicates.

• Eventual consistency: Services converge after asynchronous propagation; the UI and business process must represent intermediate states.

# Gateway, discovery and configuration

• API Gateway: Single entry for routing, authentication, TLS, coarse limits and sometimes response aggregation.

• BFF: A gateway tailored to one client type, such as web or mobile, reducing client chattiness.

• Service discovery: Maps logical service names to healthy instances; platforms such as Kubernetes provide DNS/service abstractions.

• Central configuration/secrets: Configuration is externalized; secrets belong in a secret store, not source control or images.

Do not place all business logic in the gateway. It becomes a new monolith and a central release bottleneck.

# Observability and operations

• Structured logs with trace, service, endpoint and business identifiers.

• Distributed traces across gateways, HTTP calls, messages and database work.

• Metrics for latency, traffic, errors and saturation plus business outcomes.

• Health endpoints that distinguish liveness from readiness.

• Independent CI/CD, backward-compatible contracts and safe rollout/rollback.

• Resource limits, autoscaling and failure drills for critical dependencies.

# When a modular monolith is better

Choose a modular monolith when the team is small, boundaries are still changing, operational maturity is limited, or independent scaling/deployment is not required. Strong modules and data ownership inside one deployment can later provide evidence for extraction.

# Interview-ready questions and answers

Q1. What is a microservice?

An independently deployable service aligned to a cohesive business capability, owning its data and contract and operated by a responsible team.

Q2. What are the main benefits?

Independent deployment and scaling, fault isolation, team autonomy and technology flexibility when boundaries and operations are mature.

Q3. What are the costs?

Network failure, latency, eventual consistency, contract management, distributed tracing, deployment complexity and higher infrastructure/operational effort.

Q4. Why database per service?

It preserves ownership and prevents another service from bypassing business rules or coupling releases to a shared schema.

Q5. How do services query data from multiple services?

API composition for real-time needs, replicated read models for efficient reads, or analytical stores for reporting. I avoid direct cross-service table joins.

Q6. Synchronous versus asynchronous communication?

Synchronous calls give an immediate result but couple availability and latency. Messaging decouples time and absorbs load but introduces eventual consistency and duplicate/ordering concerns.

Q7. What is a Saga?

A distributed business workflow made of local transactions. When a later step fails, compensating actions restore an acceptable business state rather than using one global transaction.

Q8. Choreography versus orchestration?

Choreography uses services reacting to events with no central coordinator; it is decoupled but flows can become hard to see. Orchestration makes the workflow explicit but centralizes coordination.

Q9. What is an API gateway?

An edge service for routing and cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, TLS and coarse rate limits. Business rules should remain in the owning service.

Q10. How do you handle duplicate messages?

Design consumers to be idempotent using message IDs, unique business keys, inbox records and atomic updates.

Q11. How do you trace a request across services?

Propagate W3C trace context/correlation through HTTP and message headers, emit spans and structured logs, and view them in a distributed tracing system.

Q12. When would you not use microservices?

When a small team and simple domain do not need independent scaling/deployment, or when operational maturity is insufficient. A modular monolith is often safer.

# Common interview traps

• Defining a microservice only as a small API.

• Sharing one database schema across “independent” services.

• Using long synchronous call chains.

• Assuming exactly-once broker delivery removes the need for idempotency.

• Putting domain logic into an API gateway.

• Ignoring deployment and observability costs.

# 60-second revision checklist

• Business capability boundaries

• Data ownership

• Sync vs async

• Saga / outbox / idempotency

• Gateway and BFF

• Eventual consistency

• Tracing and health checks

• Modular monolith alternative

title: Coding and Scenario-Based Questions
content:
GUIDE 07

Coding and Scenario-Based Questions

A repeatable problem-solving method for C#, SQL, APIs and production incidents

LEVEL Senior .NET — FOCUS Interview-ready — USE Study + revision

Interview coding is evaluated on reasoning, correctness, edge cases, complexity and communication. Scenario questions test how you diagnose uncertainty, protect production and choose trade-offs.

# What you should be able to explain

• Use a consistent method before writing code.

• Recognize dictionary, two-pointer, stack, interval and traversal patterns.

• Explain time and space complexity.

• Answer production scenarios using evidence, mitigation and prevention.

# The coding interview method

Restate the requirement and confirm input, output, constraints and examples.

Identify edge cases: null/empty, duplicates, negative values, overflow, case sensitivity and ordering.

Describe a correct baseline solution before optimizing.

Choose a data structure and explain why.

Write small, readable code and narrate key invariants.

Dry-run normal and edge cases.

State time and space complexity and mention a trade-off.

# High-value C# patterns

## Frequency map

static Dictionary<char, int> Frequency(string input)
{
    var counts = new Dictionary<char, int>();
    foreach (char c in input)
        counts[c] = counts.GetValueOrDefault(c) + 1;
    return counts; // O(n) time, O(k) space
}

## First non-repeating character

static char? FirstUnique(string input)
{
    var counts = input.GroupBy(c => c)
                      .ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Count());
    foreach (char c in input)
        if (counts[c] == 1) return c;
    return null;
}

## Two sum

static (int i, int j)? TwoSum(int[] values, int target)
{
    var seen = new Dictionary<int, int>();
    for (int i = 0; i < values.Length; i++)
    {
        int needed = target - values[i];
        if (seen.TryGetValue(needed, out int j)) return (j, i);
        seen[values[i]] = i;
    }
    return null; // O(n) time, O(n) space
}

## Balanced brackets with a stack

static bool Balanced(string text)
{
    var stack = new Stack<char>();
    var pairs = new Dictionary<char, char> { [')'] = '(', [']'] = '[', ['}'] = '{' };
    foreach (char c in text)
    {
        if (c is '(' or '[' or '{') stack.Push(c);
        else if (pairs.TryGetValue(c, out char open) &&
                 (stack.Count == 0 || stack.Pop() != open)) return false;
    }
    return stack.Count == 0;
}

# Problems you should practise

• Reverse a string and reverse words while defining Unicode expectations.

• Remove duplicates while preserving original order.

• Find duplicate numbers and missing number.

• Check palindrome while ignoring spaces/case.

• Find maximum subarray sum using Kadane’s algorithm.

• Merge overlapping intervals after sorting.

• Binary search and first/last occurrence.

• Breadth-first and depth-first traversal.

• Group anagrams using a normalized key.

• Implement an LRU cache using dictionary plus linked list.

• Flatten nested collections with SelectMany.

• Build producer/consumer flow with Channel<T> and cancellation.

Prefer a loop when it makes state and complexity clearer. LINQ is expressive for transformations, but multiple enumeration, hidden allocations or database translation can change performance and behaviour.

# SQL and API scenarios

## Slow query after data growth

Capture the actual query, parameters, duration and execution plan.

Check scans, estimates, key lookups, implicit conversions, spills and blocking.

Verify existing index order/selectivity before adding one.

Reduce rows/columns early and update statistics where appropriate.

Measure the change with representative data and monitor regression.

## Duplicate API operation after timeout

Assume the first request may have completed. Use an idempotency key, unique business constraint and stored operation result. Reconcile state rather than blindly repeating the write.

## Memory increases continuously

Compare allocation rate, heap size after full GC and retained object roots. Inspect static collections, event handlers, timers, caches, unbounded queues, large buffers and undisposed resources. Validate with a memory dump or profiler rather than guessing.

# Production scenario answer framework

Assess impact and severity: users, endpoints, error rate, latency and business consequence.

Correlate evidence: time, deployment, trace ID, logs, metrics, dependency health and database state.

Mitigate safely: rollback, feature flag, traffic reduction, failover or disable the failing path.

Reproduce or isolate the smallest failing condition.

Fix the root cause and add a regression test.

Deploy progressively and verify technical plus business metrics.

Document cause, timeline and prevention actions.

# Scenario bank

• API intermittently returns 500: Use trace IDs, exception type, dependency spans and deployment correlation; group by route/version/tenant.

• One instance is slow: Compare CPU, memory, thread pool, GC, connection pools and pod/node placement against healthy instances.

• Queue backlog grows: Compare arrival vs processing rate, consumer errors, prefetch, downstream latency and poison messages before scaling.

• Cache returns stale data: Inspect keys, invalidation timing, TTL, write ordering and per-instance vs distributed cache behaviour.

• Deployment passes but app is unhealthy: Check startup/configuration, secret access, migrations, readiness, port binding and dependency connectivity.

• Deadlock or blocking: Capture blocked sessions/threads, identify resource order, shorten transactions and make lock acquisition consistent.

# Interview-ready questions and answers

Q1. How do you start an unfamiliar coding problem?

I clarify inputs, outputs and constraints, walk through an example, identify edge cases, propose a correct baseline, then choose a data structure and optimize only where needed.

Q2. How do you explain complexity?

I define n, count dominant operations for time, and count additional data structures for space. I distinguish average from worst case when hashing or sorting is involved.

Q3. When would you use a dictionary?

For key-based lookup, counting, deduplication or complement search where average O(1) access improves an O(n²) scan to roughly O(n).

Q4. When would you use a stack?

For nested structure, reverse processing, expression parsing, DFS or matching brackets where the last item added must be handled first.

Q5. Loop versus LINQ?

I choose readability first. LINQ is excellent for declarative transformations; a loop is often clearer for complex state, early exits or allocation-sensitive hot paths.

Q6. How do you test a coding solution verbally?

I dry-run a normal case, empty/minimum input, duplicates, boundary values and a failure case, then verify complexity and mutation assumptions.

Q7. A user reports an intermittent error you cannot reproduce. What do you do?

Collect exact time, user/tenant, endpoint and trace/business ID; search logs and distributed traces; compare dependencies and deployment/config changes; then reproduce with the same inputs and environment.

Q8. How do you investigate a slow API?

Break total latency into middleware, application, database and external dependency spans; inspect query plans, thread pool, GC and resource saturation; then validate the bottleneck with measurements.

Q9. How do you handle a production incident?

Assess impact, mitigate safely, correlate evidence, isolate root cause, fix with a regression test, deploy progressively, verify metrics and document prevention.

Q10. What if requirements are ambiguous during coding?

I state the ambiguity and ask. If the interviewer wants me to proceed, I declare a reasonable assumption and show how the design changes if it is different.

Q11. What makes a senior scenario answer?

It protects users first, uses evidence, acknowledges uncertainty and trade-offs, includes safe rollout/rollback, and prevents recurrence rather than only patching symptoms.

Q12. How do you avoid overoptimizing?

Start with correct, readable code; use constraints to determine whether optimization is necessary; measure production performance before adding complexity.

# Common interview traps

• Coding before confirming requirements.

• Giving complexity without defining n.

• Using LINQ that enumerates an expensive sequence repeatedly.

• Jumping directly to “add an index” or “scale servers” without evidence.

• Fixing production before mitigating user impact.

• Claiming a timeout proves the operation failed.

# 60-second revision checklist

• Clarify -> baseline -> optimize -> test

• Dictionary / set / stack / queue / two pointers

• Time and space complexity

• Normal and edge-case dry run

• Impact -> evidence -> mitigation -> root cause

• Idempotency, slow API, memory and queue scenarios

title: Message Queues and Asynchronous Communication
content:
GUIDE 08

Message Queues and Asynchronous Communication

RabbitMQ concepts, acknowledgements, retries, dead letters, ordering and reliable delivery

LEVEL Senior .NET — FOCUS Interview-ready — USE Study + revision

A message broker decouples producers and consumers in time and helps absorb bursts. Reliability comes from application design: durable topology, publisher confirmation, acknowledgements, idempotency and observable retry/dead-letter handling.

# What you should be able to explain

• Explain exchanges, queues, bindings and routing keys.

• Design acknowledgement, retry and dead-letter behaviour.

• Handle duplicates, poison messages and ordering constraints.

• Apply outbox/inbox and consumer idempotency.

# Core broker model

• Producer: Publishes a message to an exchange.

• Exchange: Routes messages to queues based on type, bindings and routing key.

• Queue: Buffers messages until consumers process them.

• Binding: Routing rule between an exchange and queue.

• Consumer: Receives deliveries and acknowledges successful processing.

• Direct exchange: Exact routing-key match.

• Topic exchange: Pattern routing such as order.* or payment.#.

• Fanout exchange: Broadcasts to all bound queues and ignores routing key.

• Headers exchange: Routes using message header matches.

# Durability and delivery

A durable exchange/queue survives broker restart as topology; messages also need persistent publication, and operational guarantees depend on broker configuration. Publisher confirms tell the producer whether the broker accepted responsibility for a publish.

A consumer acknowledgement means processing succeeded. With manual acknowledgements, ack after the database transaction or durable side effect commits. Nack/reject can requeue or dead-letter depending on configuration.

consumer.ReceivedAsync += async (_, args) =>
{
    try
    {
        await handler.ProcessAsync(args.Body, stoppingToken);
        await channel.BasicAckAsync(args.DeliveryTag, multiple: false);
    }
    catch (TransientException)
    {
        await channel.BasicNackAsync(args.DeliveryTag, false, requeue: false);
    }
};

# Retry and dead-letter design

Immediate requeue can create a hot loop. Prefer a bounded retry policy using delayed delivery, TTL retry queues or scheduled republish, then route exhausted messages to a dead-letter queue (DLQ).

• Record attempt count and first-failure time in trusted metadata.

• Use backoff; do not retry permanent validation or schema failures.

• Alert on DLQ rate and age; provide a reviewed replay process.

• Preserve the original message ID and trace context across retries.

• Declare queue arguments consistently; changing DLX arguments for an existing queue can cause a broker precondition failure.

# Duplicates, ordering and idempotency

At-least-once delivery means a message can repeat after a consumer commits but its acknowledgement is lost. Exactly-once end-to-end business processing is rarely obtained from the broker alone.

• Idempotent consumer: Use a message ID/inbox table, unique business constraint or naturally idempotent state transition.

• Ordering: Usually guaranteed only within a queue/partition under conditions. Multiple consumers improve throughput but can reorder completion.

• Prefetch: Limits unacknowledged deliveries per consumer. Tune for message cost and fairness; too high can concentrate work and memory.

• Poison message: A permanently failing message should leave the main queue after bounded attempts.

# Outbox and event contracts

The outbox pattern stores the business change and message record in one local database transaction. A background dispatcher publishes with confirmation and marks the record sent. Consumers still deduplicate.

• Use stable event names and schemas; prefer additive evolution.

• Include event ID, occurred time, correlation/causation IDs and schema version.

• Do not publish database entities containing internal or sensitive fields.

• Monitor publish lag, queue depth, oldest-message age, processing latency, retries and DLQ count.

# Queue versus synchronous API

Use a queue when the caller does not require an immediate result, work is long-running, bursts need buffering or services should be time-decoupled. Use an API when the caller needs a current answer or immediate validation. Many workflows use both.

# Interview-ready questions and answers

Q1. Why use a message queue?

To decouple producer and consumer timing, buffer bursts, enable asynchronous workflows and isolate temporary downstream unavailability.

Q2. Exchange versus queue in RabbitMQ?

A producer publishes to an exchange. The exchange routes using bindings and routing keys; queues store deliveries for consumers.

Q3. Direct versus topic versus fanout?

Direct uses exact keys, topic uses wildcard patterns, and fanout broadcasts to every bound queue.

Q4. What is a consumer acknowledgement?

The consumer tells the broker that processing completed. I ack only after the durable business effect commits.

Q5. What are publisher confirms?

An asynchronous acknowledgement from the broker that it accepted a publication, allowing the producer to detect failed or uncertain sends.

Q6. Why avoid immediate requeue?

A persistent failure can loop at high speed, consume CPU and starve healthy messages. Bounded delayed retries plus DLQ are safer.

Q7. What is a dead-letter queue?

A queue for messages rejected, expired or exhausted after retries. It supports alerting, diagnosis and controlled replay; it should not become ignored storage.

Q8. How do you handle duplicate messages?

Make processing idempotent using a message ID/inbox record, unique constraints and atomic state transitions.

Q9. Does RabbitMQ guarantee exactly-once processing?

No end-to-end business guarantee by itself. Delivery and acknowledgements can repeat, so consumers must be idempotent.

Q10. How do you preserve ordering?

Use one ordered queue/partition and compatible consumer strategy for the ordering key. Parallel consumers increase throughput but can reorder completion.

Q11. What is prefetch?

The maximum number of unacknowledged deliveries the broker sends to a consumer. It balances throughput, fairness and memory.

Q12. What metrics do you monitor?

Queue depth, oldest-message age, publish/consume rates, unacknowledged count, processing latency, retry/DLQ rates and consumer failures.

# Common interview traps

• Acknowledging before database commit.

• Requeueing poison messages forever.

• Assuming durable queue alone makes every message safe.

• Changing arguments on an existing RabbitMQ queue and expecting redeclaration to update it.

• Depending on global ordering with multiple consumers.

• Replaying a DLQ without fixing or isolating the cause.

# 60-second revision checklist

• Exchange / binding / queue / routing key

• Direct / topic / fanout

• Durability and confirms

• Manual ack after commit

• Bounded retry and DLQ

• Idempotent consumer

• Outbox/inbox

• Prefetch, ordering and metrics

title: Docker and Deployment Fundamentals
content:
GUIDE 09

Docker and Deployment Fundamentals

Images, containers, multi-stage .NET builds, Compose, configuration and secure runtime practices

LEVEL Senior .NET — FOCUS Interview-ready — USE Study + revision

Docker packages an application and runtime dependencies into an immutable image. A container is a running isolated process created from that image. Production readiness depends on configuration, networking, storage, health and security—not only a working Dockerfile.

# What you should be able to explain

• Explain image layers, containers and registries.

• Build a small production .NET image with multi-stage builds.

• Configure ports, networks, volumes, environment and secrets.

• Describe health checks, logging and deployment concerns.

# Core concepts

• Dockerfile: Instructions used to build an image.

• Image: Immutable layered filesystem plus metadata.

• Container: A running process isolated with namespaces/cgroups and configured from an image.

• Registry: Stores and distributes versioned images.

• Volume: Persistent data managed outside the writable container layer.

• Network: Provides service-to-service connectivity and DNS names.

Containers share the host kernel; they are lighter than virtual machines but are not identical to VMs. Treat the image as immutable and replace containers for deployment rather than patching them manually.

# Multi-stage .NET Dockerfile

A build stage contains the SDK and compilers; the final stage contains only the runtime and published output. This reduces image size and attack surface. Match the image version to the project’s target framework.

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY ["OrderService/OrderService.csproj", "OrderService/"]
RUN dotnet restore "OrderService/OrderService.csproj"
COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish "OrderService/OrderService.csproj" \
    -c Release -o /app/publish --no-restore

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0 AS final
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/publish .
USER $APP_UID
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "OrderService.dll"]

• Copy project files and restore before source code to improve layer-cache reuse.

• Use .dockerignore to exclude bin, obj, .git, secrets and unrelated files.

• Pin a supported base version and rebuild regularly for security patches.

• Run as a non-root user when the base image and environment support it.

# Runtime configuration

• Ports: EXPOSE documents a port; -p or the orchestrator publishes host access.

• Environment: Use environment variables/config providers for non-secret configuration.

• Secrets: Inject from a secret store or platform secret mechanism; do not bake into an image or Dockerfile.

• Networking: Inside Compose, call another service by service name and container port, not localhost.

• Storage: Use a volume or external service for state that must survive container replacement.

• Logs: Write structured logs to stdout/stderr for collection by the platform.

# Docker Compose for local integration

services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      ConnectionStrings__RabbitMq: amqp://guest:guest@rabbitmq:5672
    depends_on:
      rabbitmq:
        condition: service_healthy

  rabbitmq:
    image: rabbitmq:management
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "rabbitmq-diagnostics", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

depends_on controls startup order but does not replace application-level retry and readiness. Dependencies can fail after startup as well.

# Health, security and deployment

• Liveness: Can the process make progress, or should it be restarted? Avoid depending on every downstream service.

• Readiness: Can this instance receive traffic now? It may include critical dependency/startup checks.

• Security: Use minimal images, non-root user, read-only filesystem where practical, vulnerability scanning and least privilege.

• Graceful shutdown: Handle SIGTERM, stop accepting work and finish/cancel within the platform grace period.

• Deployment: Tag images immutably, promote the same tested artifact, roll out gradually and keep rollback available.

Docker Compose coordinates local or small multi-container environments. Kubernetes/managed container platforms add scheduling, desired state, scaling, service discovery and rollout controls.

# Interview-ready questions and answers

Q1. Image versus container?

An image is an immutable template of filesystem layers and metadata. A container is a running isolated process created from an image with runtime configuration.

Q2. Why use a multi-stage build?

The SDK stays in the build stage while only published output and runtime enter the final stage, reducing size and attack surface.

Q3. What is the Docker build context?

The directory sent to the builder. A small context plus .dockerignore improves speed and prevents accidental inclusion of secrets or unnecessary files.

Q4. EXPOSE versus port publishing?

EXPOSE documents the intended container port. Publishing maps a host/platform port to it and is what makes it reachable externally.

Q5. Why does localhost fail between containers?

Inside a container, localhost refers to that same container. Services communicate through the container network using the target service DNS name and port.

Q6. Where should configuration and secrets live?

Non-secret configuration is injected at runtime; secrets come from a protected secret store/platform mechanism. Neither should be baked into the image.

Q7. Volume versus bind mount?

A volume is managed by Docker and suited to persistent container data. A bind mount maps a specific host path and is common in development but couples to host layout.

Q8. Liveness versus readiness?

Liveness asks whether the process should be restarted. Readiness asks whether it should receive traffic. A failing dependency may remove readiness without requiring process restart.

Q9. Why run as non-root?

It reduces impact if the process is compromised and supports least privilege.

Q10. How do containers log?

Applications normally emit structured logs to stdout/stderr; the container platform collects and forwards them.

Q11. Docker Compose versus Kubernetes?

Compose defines and runs multi-container applications, mainly for local/smaller use. Kubernetes provides cluster scheduling, desired state, scaling, service discovery and controlled rollout.

Q12. How do you deploy safely?

Build an immutable tagged image, scan/test it, promote the same artifact, inject environment configuration, use readiness and progressive rollout, verify metrics and retain rollback.

# Common interview traps

• Putting secrets in Dockerfile ENV or image layers.

• Using localhost for another container.

• Using the SDK image as the final production image.

• Storing important data only in the writable container layer.

• Making liveness fail whenever a downstream service is temporarily unavailable.

• Using the mutable latest tag as the only production identity.

# 60-second revision checklist

• Image / container / registry

• Layer caching and .dockerignore

• Multi-stage SDK -> runtime

• Ports and container DNS

• Volumes and externalized config

• Secrets and non-root

• Liveness/readiness and graceful shutdown

• Immutable rollout/rollback

title: CI/CD Fundamentals
content:
GUIDE 10

CI/CD Fundamentals

Build, test, package, deploy and rollback with Azure Pipelines-style examples

LEVEL Senior .NET — FOCUS Interview-ready — USE Study + revision

CI/CD turns source changes into repeatable, testable releases. A strong pipeline produces one immutable artifact, promotes it through environments, protects secrets, enforces quality gates and makes rollback or roll-forward safe.

# What you should be able to explain

• Differentiate continuous integration, delivery and deployment.

• Explain stages, jobs, steps, agents and artifacts.

• Design environment promotion, approvals and rollback.

• Troubleshoot pipelines and protect supply-chain secrets.

# Core definitions

• Continuous integration: Frequently merge small changes and automatically restore, build, test and analyze them.

• Continuous delivery: Keep a validated artifact deployable; production release may require approval.

• Continuous deployment: Automatically deploy every qualifying change to production.

• Pipeline as code: Version the workflow with source, review changes and reproduce execution.

# Pipeline anatomy

• Trigger: Push, pull request, schedule or manual execution.

• Stage: Major boundary such as Build, Test, Staging or Production.

• Job: Unit of work assigned to an agent.

• Step/task: Command or reusable action inside a job.
